top_fixes.title: Calibrator is fit on in-sample pipeline probabilities (pipeline refit on ALL data first)
top_fixes.issue: _fit_sklearn refits the shipped pipeline on the FULL dataset (line 687) with no tail excluded, then train(calibrate=True) fits fit_calibration on X[cal_lo:cal_hi] (line 989), whose raw probs come from self.pipeline.predict_proba on those same in-sample rows (line 1157). The calibrator learns a map from memorized (over-optimistic) probabilities to labels, so at serve time it under-corrects real out-of-sample overconfidence — defeating the purpose of the calibration rework. Two findings report this (rated high and critical); it is the same root leak.
top_fixes.fix: Carve a genuine tail holdout out of the final refit: fit self.pipeline on X_arr[:-n_hold] (n_hold >= calibrate_frac), and feed fit_calibration out-of-sample probabilities from that model (or use cross_val_predict). This is the shared root fix for ranks 1, 2, 4, 5.

top_fixes.title: Reported 'holdout' RPS/log-loss/Brier are in-sample (scored with the all-data pipeline)
top_fixes.issue: The pipeline is refit on the full dataset at line 687, then the same fitted pipe scores Xte = X_arr[-test_size:] (last 20%) at line 734. Those rows were in the final refit, so rps_/log_loss_/brier_ are measured on training data. The comment at 724-725 ('a genuine, untouched holdout') is false. With a bootstrapped RF leg this makes the headline metrics and the ~0.19-0.21 RPS comparison dramatically optimistic.
top_fixes.fix: Score the tail with a pipeline that never trained on it (the rank-1 holdout carve-out), OR accumulate out-of-fold predictions inside _evaluate_pipeline and score once. Correct the misleading comment. Note (finding at line 730): the metric holdout overlaps the calibrator's fit slice, so calibrated recompute must score only the disjoint second half (cal_hi:), mirroring evaluate.py.

top_fixes.title: Flask runs debug=True bound to 0.0.0.0 — network-exposed Werkzeug debugger (RCE)
top_fixes.issue: app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True) is hardcoded with no env gating. Any unhandled route exception (see rank 14: /predict has none) opens the interactive traceback console, whose eval shell allows arbitrary Python execution, reachable from any host on the LAN. Highest-severity issue in the codebase; three findings converge here.
top_fixes.fix: app.run(host=os.getenv("HOST","127.0.0.1"), port=int(os.getenv("PORT","5000")), debug=os.getenv("FLASK_DEBUG")=="1"). import os. For real exposure use a WSGI server with debug off.

top_fixes.title: evaluate.py grades the shipped model on rows it trained on
top_fixes.issue: evaluate.py loads the pipeline (trained on ALL data) and scores model.apply_calibration(model.pipeline.predict_proba(Xte)) on the second half of the last 20%, which was in the pipeline's training set. Every 'honest evaluation' number — RPS, log-loss, per-league accuracy/F1/draw-recall, and the reliability curve driving the dashboard — is in-sample and overstates real performance.
top_fixes.fix: Same root as rank 1: exclude the eval slice from the pipeline's final refit and persist n_hold (or the date boundary) so evaluate.py's slice lines up with what was actually withheld. Then the reliability curve reflects served behaviour.

top_fixes.title: Persisted/dashboard rps/log-loss/brier are UNCALIBRATED but the model ships calibrated
top_fixes.issue: _compute_prob_metrics scores raw pipe.predict_proba(Xte) before fit_calibration ever runs, so saved rps_/log_loss_/brier_ (and get_metrics/dashboard) describe probabilities no user sees. predict() and evaluate.py both apply calibration, so evaluation.json's same-named metrics disagree with model.json's. Whether calibration helped is invisible.
top_fixes.fix: After fit_calibration in train(), recompute the prob-metrics through apply_calibration on the disjoint second-half of the holdout (indices cal_hi:), never the calibrator's own fit slice. Or keep raw fields renamed (rps_raw_) and add calibrated counterparts as the primary reported number.

top_fixes.title: Season-gap Elo regression applied only in training, never at serving (skew on the top feature)
top_fixes.issue: Training pulls a team's Elo 10% toward 1500 after a >45-day (ELO_SEASON_GAP) idle before computing home_elo/elo_diff (lines 392-396). Serving reads home.get('elo', ELO_START) verbatim with no date/regression (line 670-671; compute_team_stats stores un-regressed elo at 878/891). Every off-season prediction (the normal case) serves an un-regressed Elo, systematically over-rating favourites on elo_diff/abs_elo_diff/tightness — the model's most important feature. This is the recurring train/serve bug, ACTIVE today, and the guard test's 8-20 day fixture never exercises a >45-day gap.
top_fixes.fix: Persist each team's last match date in compute_team_stats; give prepare_prediction_features an as_of_date (default = max dataset date); apply the same ELO_SEASON_GAP/ELO_SEASON_REGRESS rule via the shared _days_between helper before building elo features. Add a guard-test case with two served matches >45 days apart.

top_fixes.title: SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif) has no random_state — nondeterministic feature selection
top_fixes.issue: mutual_info_classif uses a kNN estimator with random noise and random_state=None, so the winning select_k, the surviving feature set, and persisted feature_importances_ all vary run to run — on both the tuning scoring and the final 167k-row fit. top_fixes.title: Recency scaling + global renormalization silently undoes the balanced class-weight correction
top_fixes.issue: sw = balanced * rw; sw *= len/sum applies only a global scalar, so per-class totals no longer equalise — recency reweights the classes as a side effect. If draws skew older (plausible: 8 leagues added only for recent seasons), the balanced draw-recall correction is quietly weakened. Present in both CV folds (410) and final refit (685). NOTE: currently latent because recency is off by default (rank 16), but must be fixed before enabling recency.
top_fixes.fix: Renormalize PER CLASS after sw*=rw: scale sw[y==c] so each class sums to n/n_classes; drop the global rescale. Apply at both sites.

all_findings.title: Serving recomputes Dixon-Coles probabilities with the module rho, ignoring any tuned dc_rho used in training
all_findings.issue: The dc_* probabilities (dc_home_prob/dc_draw_prob/dc_away_prob) AND their derived draw-signal features (dc_entropy, and the dc probs feeding tightness) are recomputed from scratch at prediction time. Training builds them via DixonColesRatings.predict, which passes self.rho into match_probabilities (dixon_coles.py:121-124), and self.rho is settable through add_form_features(dc_rho=...) (data_processor.py:206,212). Serving calls dixon_coles.match_probabilities(...) at data_processor.py:728 with NO rho argument, so it silently falls back to the module constant DC_RHO (dixon_coles.py:92). rho is never persisted with the model nor plumbed through app.py:201 -> prepare_prediction_features. Today this is harmless only because the shipped model was trained with the default (rating_constants_tuning.json chose dc_rho=-0.1 == DC_RHO and csv_data_loader.py:667 / main.py:80 pass no override). But it is exactly the recurring failure mode: retrain with a tuned rho and every live dc_* / dc_entropy / tightness value is computed from a different low-score correlation than the model learned, with nothing catching it. rho, unlike dc_k, is re-evaluated at serve time (the ratings themselves are stored as *_dc_attack_post, but the probability grid is not), so it is the one DC parameter that must be kept identical across train and serve.
all_findings.fix: Persist the trained dc_rho alongside the model (main.py already persists leagues/dates/h2h), give prepare_prediction_features an explicit rho parameter defaulting to dixon_coles.DC_RHO, and pass the persisted value through at data_processor.py:728. Alternatively store the effective rho on team_stats in compute_team_stats and read it here. Add a test that trains with a non-default dc_rho and asserts the live dc_home_prob equals a hand-computed match_probabilities(..., rho=that_rho).
all_findings.why_it_matters: This is the precise train/serve-skew pattern the codebase has been bitten by five times: a feature computed one way while training and another way while serving, returning confident but wrong probabilities, with no guard test covering it.
all_findings.reason: data_processor.py:728 calls dixon_coles.match_probabilities(...) with only attack/defense/league-base args — no rho kwarg — so it hits the `rho: float = None` default (dixon_coles.py:82) and resolves to `DC_RHO if rho is None else rho` (dixon_coles.py:92), i.e. the hardcoded -0.10 module constant. Meanwhile the training path add_form_features(dc_rho=...) (data_processor.py:181,206,212) builds DixonColesRatings(k=dc_k, rho=dc_rho) whose self.rho is genuinely settable and flows into match_probabilities via the ratings object's predict/update path (dixon_coles.py:113-124). There is no persistence of an effective dc_rho anywhere in the repo (grep shows it only in data_processor.py's training default/signature and in rating_constants_tuning.json, which hardcodes -0.1 for every league, matching DC_RHO by coincidence, not by wiring). So today's shipped model is unaffected only because the tuned value equals the default; the mechanism described (rho silently reverting to the module constant at serve time if ever tuned differently, corrupting dc_home_prob/draw/away, dc_exp_home/away, and downstream dc_entropy/tightness/evenness features) is real and unguarded.
all_findings.corrected_fix: Fix as proposed is accurate: persist the trained dc_rho (and dc_k, since the same store-nothing pattern applies to it, though ratings themselves are persisted via *_dc_attack_post) alongside the model artifacts already saved in main.py (leagues/dates/h2h), add an explicit rho parameter to prepare_prediction_features defaulting to dixon_coles.DC_RHO for backward compatibility with older team_stats.json, thread it through to the data_processor.py:728 call, and add a regression test that trains with a non-default dc_rho and asserts live dc_home_prob matches a hand-computed match_probabilities(..., rho=that_rho) rather than the default.

all_findings.title: New draw-signal features have no targeted guard-test coverage; the alignment-test docstring is stale
all_findings.issue: TestLiveFeaturesMatchTrainingDistribution is the designated guard for the recurring bug, but it does not specifically exercise the NEW draw_signal features (dc_entropy, dc_total_exp_goals, tightness). Its docstring (lines 584-587) still says the bug 'has bitten four times — team names, head-to-head, squad values, and season_progress' and never mentions the 5th instance (the venue-split form/goals/gd_5 block, which the code comment at data_processor.py:630 and test at line 629 explicitly call the 'fifth instance') nor the draw-signal family. The only coverage the draw-signal features get is test_no_live_feature_is_wildly_outside_training_range (line 675), which is very weak: it SKIPS any feature that is constant in the fixture (line 685) and passes anything within [min-span, max+span] — a 2x-span tolerance that a real skew (e.g. a collapsed/degenerate dc_entropy=0 or tightness=0) could easily sit inside. There is no assertion anywhere that the live dc_entropy/tightness are non-degenerate or equal the shared-helper output.
all_findings.fix: Add explicit assertions in TestLiveFeaturesMatchTrainingDistribution that the live vector's dc_entropy > 0 and 0 < tightness <= 1 (they would be 0 if the DC probs collapsed or the inputs went degenerate at serve), and ideally that live[name.index('dc_entropy')] equals draw_signal_features(...) recomputed from the same serve-side dc probs/elo/form. Update the docstring to list the venue-split block and draw-signal features so the guard's intent matches the current feature set.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The stated purpose of this test class is to automatically catch the whole class of populated-in-training / degenerate-at-serve features. The newest, least-battle-tested features (the ones this audit was asked to scrutinize hardest) are the ones it does not actually assert on.
all_findings.reason: Read tests/test_data_processor.py:578-689 directly. The class docstring at lines 579-587 literally says "It has bitten four times — team names, head-to-head, squad values, and season_progress" with no mention of the venue-split block (5th instance) or the draw-signal features, even though data_processor.py:630-633 explicitly labels the venue-split form/goals/gd_5 capture as the "fifth instance" of this exact bug family. Confirmed via grep that draw_signal_features (data_processor.py:138-165) produces dc_entropy/dc_total_exp_goals/tightness, wired into training at line 485 and serving at lines 758-762 — these are new, untested-by-name features. The only test that touches them at all is test_no_live_feature_is_wildly_outside_training_range (line 675-689), which (a) skips any feature with lo==hi in the fixture (line 684-685) and (b) uses a 2x-span tolerance window [lo-span, hi+span] (line 686-687) that would happily pass a collapsed dc_entropy=0 or tightness=0 sitting inside that widened band. No test asserts dc_entropy>0, 0<tightness<=1, or recomputes draw_signal_features on the serve side to check equality with the live vector. All five specific-mechanism tests (599-673) target only season_progress and venue-split form; none target the draw-signal trio.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is fine and directly actionable — no correction needed. Concretely: in TestLiveFeaturesMatchTrainingDistribution, add a test that (1) calls prepare_prediction_features on the built fixture, locates the dc_entropy/dc_total_exp_goals/tightness indices via names, and asserts dc_entropy > 0 and 0 < tightness <= 1 (both would be 0 only if DC probs or elo/form diffs went degenerate at serve time, e.g. probs defaulting to a delta distribution or elo_diff/form_diff both reading as missing); (2) independently recomputes draw_signal_features(...) from the same dc probs/elo/form values used at serve time and asserts the three live values equal that recomputation exactly, mirroring how test_venue_split_form_comes_from_the_matching_venue cross-checks against the row data. Also update the docstring to enumerate all five bitten instances (team names, head-to-head, squad values, season_progress, venue-split form/goals/gd_5 block) plus a forward-looking note that any new shared-computation feature (like draw_signal_features) needs an explicit equality/non-degeneracy assertion here, not just the loose range check.

all_findings.title: Silent flat-key fallbacks in prepare_prediction_features can mask a venue-split skew with no error
all_findings.issue: The venue-split reads use silent fallbacks: home.get('home_form', home.get('form', 0)) at line 681 (and lines 682-688, 707-708). The comment (lines 673-679) explains these exist so a team_stats.json written before the venue keys existed 'degrades to the old behaviour instead of serving zeros'. But 'the old behaviour' IS the exact venue skew that was fixed — flat 'form'/'gd_5' hold whichever venue the team's most recent match happened to be at, which is the wrong venue about half the time. If team_stats is ever stale (a pre-venge-key team_stats.json, or rows not passed through the updated add_form_features), serving silently reverts to the buggy path with no exception and no test failure, because the fallback swallows the missing key. Since data was just regenerated the venue keys are present today, so this is latent, not active.
all_findings.fix: Either drop the flat-key fallback and let a missing venue key surface (KeyError or an explicit 0 that the range guard would flag), or add a one-time assertion/log in compute_team_stats that every team with home history has home_form/home_gd_5/etc. set, so a stale stats file fails loudly instead of silently skewing.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A fallback that maps a missing new key onto the precise value the fix was meant to eliminate re-opens the original skew the moment the stats artifact and the code drift out of sync — the same silent-degeneracy shape as the documented bugs.
all_findings.reason: data_processor.py:680-688,707-708 exactly matches the finding: home.get("home_form", home.get("form", 0)) and the parallel home_gd_5/away_gd_5 fallbacks. The comment at 673-679 explicitly confirms the intent: a team_stats.json predating the venue-split keys silently "degrades to the old behaviour" (flat form/gd_5) rather than erroring. compute_team_stats (line 768+) does default home_form/home_gd_5 to 0 in its base dict (lines 793, 797) and always writes them via the KEY_MAP-style loop (lines 832-836), so under the current pipeline the venue keys are always present and the fallback path is dead code today — this matches the finding's own assessment that it's "latent, not active." The risk is real for any future or externally-generated team_stats.json that lacks these keys, since dict.get with a chained default swallows the KeyError with no log/assertion, silently reintroducing the exact venue skew the fix addressed. This is the same class of failure as the four other documented train/serve skew bugs in HANDOFF.md. Severity "low" is fair given it requires a stale/malformed artifact to trigger, and the proposed fix (assert/log completeness in compute_team_stats, or let missing keys surface) is sound and proportionate.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is fine as-is; slight refinement: add an assertion/log at the end of compute_team_stats (after the loop around line 832-836) that for every team with any home-venue matches, home_form/home_gd_5/home_goals_scored_avg/home_goals_conceded_avg/home_matches_played keys exist and are non-None (they will be, since compute_team_stats always sets them from the base dict) — the real protection should instead live in prepare_prediction_features or wherever team_stats.json is loaded from disk: validate on load that a sample of teams have the venue-split keys present, and raise/log loudly if not, rather than only guarding compute_team_stats's own output which is already correct by construction.

all_findings.title: Reported "holdout" RPS/log-loss/Brier are in-sample, not held out
all_findings.issue: In _fit_sklearn the pipeline is refit on the FULL dataset at line 687 (pipe.fit(X_arr, y_arr, ...)), and then the same fitted `pipe` is used at line 734 to compute prob metrics on Xte = X_arr[-test_size:] (last 20%). Those tail rows were part of the final refit, so rps_, log_loss_ and brier_ are measured on training data, not a holdout. The comment at lines 724-725 ('a genuine, untouched holdout ... never seen during CV-fold fitting') is false for the shipped pipeline: CV folds never test the tail out-of-fold, but the final model that produces these numbers was trained on it. With a bootstrapped RandomForest leg this in-sample log-loss/RPS is dramatically optimistic vs. what a user ever sees. Only cv_mean/cv_rps (from _evaluate_pipeline's purged folds) are genuinely out-of-sample; every probability metric surfaced as the headline 'holdout' number is not.
all_findings.fix: Do not score the tail with the all-data pipeline. Either (a) compute rps_/log_loss_/brier_ from out-of-fold predictions produced inside _evaluate_pipeline (accumulate proba for the scored folds and score once), or (b) fit a separate pipeline on X_arr[:-test_size] purely to produce the tail metrics, keeping the all-data pipeline only for serving. Update the misleading comment at 724-725.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The single number the training pipeline advertises as its honest holdout skill is measured on memorized rows, so model comparisons and the ~0.19-0.21 SOTA claim are being made against an inflated baseline.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:686-689 refits `pipe` on the entire dataset (`pipe.fit(X_arr, y_arr, clf__sample_weight=sw_full)` with no train/test split), and that same `pipe` object is then used at line 734 (`proba = pipe.predict_proba(Xte)`) where `Xte = X_arr[-test_size:]` (line 730) — the last 20% of rows, which were included in the full-data fit at 687. So every probabilistic metric derived from this (`self.log_loss_`, `self.brier_`, `self.rps_` via `_compute_prob_metrics` at 735/762-766) is computed on rows the model was trained on, i.e. in-sample, not held out. The comment at lines 724-725 explicitly claims this is "a genuine, untouched holdout... never seen during CV-fold fitting" — that phrasing is misleading because while it's true the tail wasn't scored out-of-fold during CV, it absolutely was seen by the exact pipeline object used to score it, via the full-data refit two blocks above. Only `cv_res`/`self.cv_rps`/`self.macro_f1_` (populated from `_evaluate_pipeline` at line 675, which runs proper purged CV folds before the full refit) are genuinely out-of-sample. This matches the finding's mechanism exactly.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix (b) is the simplest robust one: before the full-data refit at line 687, fit a separate throwaway pipeline on `X_arr[:-test_size]` / `y_arr[:-test_size]` (with matching sample-weight balancing/recency scaling restricted to that slice) solely to call `predict_proba` on `Xte` for `_compute_prob_metrics`; keep `self.pipeline = pipe` as the full-data-fit production model for serving. Alternatively (a), accumulate out-of-fold probabilities inside `_evaluate_pipeline` for the CV folds and score log-loss/Brier/RPS from those instead of introducing a second holdout-only fit — this reuses work already being done and avoids training a throwaway model. Either way, correct the comment at 724-725 to state that this is computed either on a held-out refit or from out-of-fold CV predictions, not from the shipped full-data pipeline.

all_findings.title: Calibrator is fit on in-sample (over-confident) pipeline probabilities
all_findings.issue: train(calibrate=True) calls fit_calibration(X[cal_lo:cal_hi], ...) at line 989 on the first half of the last 20%. fit_calibration derives its raw probabilities from self.pipeline.predict_proba (line 1157), but self.pipeline was already refit on ALL data (line 687), including that calibration slice. The calibrator therefore learns a map from IN-SAMPLE probabilities (systematically over-confident, since the base model partly memorized these rows) to labels. At serve time the inputs are genuinely out-of-sample and less confident, so the fitted Dirichlet/Platt map is mis-specified and will under-correct — the opposite of what recalibration is meant to do. The fit-vs-eval split between train() and evaluate.py is correctly disjoint (cal = first half, eval = second half), so this is not a fit/eval overlap; the leak is that the calibrator never sees realistic out-of-sample probabilities at all.
all_findings.fix: Feed the calibrator out-of-fold probabilities for the calibration slice: either fit the pipeline on data strictly before cal_lo and predict the calibration slice with THAT model, or exclude the calibration slice from the pipeline's final refit, or use cross_val_predict to generate the raw probabilities passed into fit_calibration.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The calibration step exists specifically to make displayed probabilities mean what they say; fitting it on memorized probabilities defeats its purpose and can leave live probabilities as miscalibrated as before.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:687 `pipe.fit(X_arr, y_arr, clf__sample_weight=sw_full)` refits the pipeline on the entire dataset passed to train() — there is no split that excludes the tail. train() then computes cal_lo/cal_hi as a slice of the same X/y (last 20% window, first half) at lines 984-987, and calls `self.fit_calibration(X[cal_lo:cal_hi], y[cal_lo:cal_hi])` at line 989. Inside fit_calibration, line 1157 does `raw = self.pipeline.predict_proba(np.asarray(X_holdout, ...))` — but self.pipeline is the pipe that was already fit on X_arr including exactly these rows (line 691: `self.pipeline = pipe`). So the calibrator's input probabilities are in-sample/memorized, not genuinely out-of-fold. The separate downstream evaluate.py holdout (second half of the tail, non-overlapping with the calibration slice) avoids fit/eval overlap for scoring purposes, but does not fix the calibrator's own training data being in-sample relative to the base pipeline. Severity is arguably tempered by tree/ensemble models' bounded ability to fully memorize continuous engineered features with balanced class weights and regularization, but the mechanism described is real and verified in code.
all_findings.corrected_fix: Generate out-of-fold probabilities for the calibration slice instead of using the fully-refit self.pipeline: fit a clone of the pipeline (same tree_params/voting_weights/select_k) on X_arr[:cal_lo] only (i.e., all data strictly before the calibration window, preserving temporal order and the existing purge_gap convention), call .predict_proba on X[cal_lo:cal_hi] with that model, and pass those probabilities into fit_calibration (which would need a param to accept precomputed raw probabilities rather than always calling self.pipeline.predict_proba internally). Then keep the final self.pipeline as the full refit (line 687-691) for serving, since that part is correct/desirable for production quality.

all_findings.title: evaluate.py grades the shipped model on rows it trained on
all_findings.issue: evaluate.py loads the saved pipeline (trained on ALL of processed_data in train_model_csv) and at line 257 scores proba = model.apply_calibration(model.pipeline.predict_proba(Xte)) on Xte = X[-n_test:] (the second half of the last 20%, lines 245-252). Those rows were in the pipeline's training set, so every metric this 'honest evaluation' emits — RPS, log-loss, per-league accuracy/macro-F1/draw-recall, and the reliability curve — is in-sample. The reliability curve in particular will look far better calibrated than reality because the base model fits training rows tightly. The draw_threshold_curve tune/score split (first vs second half of this slice) is internally disjoint and fine, but it operates on the same in-sample probabilities, so its absolute numbers are still optimistic.
all_findings.fix: Evaluate on data excluded from the pipeline's final fit. Persist which rows were used for the final refit (or hold out a genuine tail from training) and have evaluate.py load a model whose pipeline never saw the evaluation slice — mirroring the fix for the _fit_sklearn holdout metrics.
all_findings.why_it_matters: evaluate.py is the artifact whose whole stated purpose is answering 'do the probabilities mean what they say'; as written it cannot answer that because it tests on the training set, so the dashboard reliability curve and per-league numbers overstate real-world performance.
all_findings.reason: main.py:136 calls model.train(X, y, ...) with the FULL processed dataset (no pre-split holdout carved out). Inside model_trainer.py _fit_sklearn, line 678's comment literally says "Refit on all data" and line 687 does pipe.fit(X_arr, y_arr, clf__sample_weight=sw_full) where X_arr/y_arr is the entire dataset — so the shipped pipeline's RF/HistGB/ensemble legs are fit on every row, including the last 20% tail. Only the calibrator layer is deliberately kept honest: train()'s calibrate branch (model_trainer.py:983-989) fits fit_calibration on X[cal_lo:cal_hi] = the FIRST half of the last calibrate_frac (20%) slice, and evaluate.py:245-257 scores on the SECOND half of that same tail slice via model.apply_calibration(model.pipeline.predict_proba(Xte)). So the calibration mapping itself is evaluated on genuinely unseen-by-the-calibrator rows, but model.pipeline (the base estimator whose raw probabilities feed the calibrator) was already fit on those exact Xte rows in the earlier full refit. Every metric evaluate.py reports — RPS, log-loss, accuracy, macro-F1, draw-recall, reliability curve, per-league breakdown, and the draw-threshold tune/test split — is therefore computed from a base pipeline that already trained on the scoring rows. Tree ensembles (RF especially, HistGB to a lesser degree) fit training rows more confidently/accurately than genuinely unseen data, so these numbers overstate real-world calibration and skill. The finding's diagnosis and file:line citation are accurate.
all_findings.corrected_fix: Carve out the tail holdout BEFORE the final refit, not just before calibration. E.g. in train(), reserve the last max(calibrate_frac, HOLDOUT_FRACTION) fraction of X/y (a slice large enough to cover both the calibration-fit half and evaluate.py's test half) and exclude it entirely from the pipe.fit(X_arr, y_arr) call at model_trainer.py:687 (fit only on X_arr[:-n_hold], y_arr[:-n_hold]), while still using the full data for the CV search/_evaluate_pipeline diagnostics if desired. Persist n_hold (or the holdout's date boundary) alongside the model so evaluate.py's slice indexing continues to line up with what was actually excluded from the refit, rather than assuming index alignment implies data exclusion as it does today.

all_findings.title: Argentina (ar.1) misclassified as pure calendar-year; split-year seasons silently ingest 0 matches from the new feed
all_findings.issue: ar.1 is placed in CALENDAR_YEAR_LEAGUES (line 109-111), so _fd_couk_new_season_label() (line 122-123) always produces a single-year label and parse_fd_couk_new_csv() (line 353) filters the feed by exact Season-string equality. But the real ar.1 feed (verified in data_cache/all_fdcouk_new_ar.1.csv) MIXES formats: its Season column contains '2012/2013','2013/2014','2014','2015','2016','2016/2017','2017/2018','2018/2019','2019/2020','2020',...'2026'. The labels the code generates for AVAILABLE_SEASONS are '2013','2014',...,'2026'. Result: label '2013' matches 0 rows (feed has '2012/2013'), and labels '2017','2018','2019' each match 0 rows (feed only has '2016/2017','2017/2018','2018/2019'). For 2013-14 and 2019-20 the code loads only the small calendar torneo ('2014'=190,'2020'=134) and silently drops the split-year torneo rows ('2013/2014'=383,'2019/2020'=276) with no fallback. The 2016-17/2017-18/2018-19 zero-match seasons survive ONLY because the loader falls through to the footballcsv mirror (cached 2016-17_ar.1.csv etc. confirmed present), a source documented as stale (caps at 2023-24, external repo) — if it disappears, three seasons of Argentine data vanish. So ~660 matches are dropped outright and ~1140 more depend on a fragile stale fallback.
all_findings.fix: Do not filter ar.1 (or any calendar-year league) by exact Season-string equality. Parse the calendar year from each row's Date column and match rows whose Date-year equals the target calendar year, OR accept BOTH the calendar-year label AND the split-year label (e.g. treat '2016-17' as matching Season in {'2017','2016/2017'}). This handles Argentina's mixed labels without double-counting (each match has one Date) and removes reliance on the stale footballcsv mirror.
all_findings.why_it_matters: ~35% of the Argentine match history is either dropped or only reachable via a stale external mirror; this is the exact 'silently ingests 0 matches' recurring-bug shape called out in the audit brief, for a league the model advertises as supported.
all_findings.reason: Verified directly against data_cache/all_fdcouk_new_ar.1.csv (Season column value counts): 2012/2013=381, 2013/2014=383, 2014=190, 2015=468, 2016=242, 2016/2017=450, 2017/2018=378, 2018/2019=324, 2019/2020=276, 2020=134, 2021=501, 2022=581, 2023=582, 2024=581, 2025=510, 2026=257 — confirming the feed mixes split-year and pure-calendar-year labels exactly as the finding states. csv_data_loader.py:109-111 puts ar.1 in CALENDAR_YEAR_LEAGUES, so _fd_couk_new_season_label (line 114-124) always emits a single 4-digit end-year label, and parse_fd_couk_new_csv (line 353) does exact-string equality `row.get('Season','').strip() != season_label`. Mapping AVAILABLE_SEASONS (line 39-42) through the label function reproduces the finding's numbers precisely: season '2016-17'->'2017' (0 feed rows, since feed only has '2016/2017'), '2017-18'->'2018' (0 rows), '2018-19'->'2019' (0 rows) — these three (450+378+324=1152 rows) yield zero matches from the new feed and load_season_league_data (line 541-549) falls through to the footballcsv mirror, which is documented in-code (line 24-26, 29-31) as capped at 2023-24 and confirmed present in cache (2016-17_ar.1.csv, 2017-18_ar.1.csv, 2018-19_ar.1.csv). Seasons '2013-14'->'2014' and '2019-20'->'2020' each match only the smaller calendar-torneo bucket (190 and 134 rows respectively) while silently dropping the larger split-year bucket ('2013/2014'=383, '2019/2020'=276, total 659 ≈ the finding's '~660 dropped outright'). All the finding's specific figures check out against the actual cached feed content and the actual matching code path.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is directionally right; refine it: rather than parsing Date-year (adds ambiguity for Feb/Jan boundary matches and duplicate-counting risk if both a calendar and split-year torneo overlap in months), have _fd_couk_new_season_label return the acceptable label SET for ar.1 specifically (e.g. {'2017','2016/2017'} for '2016-17'), and change parse_fd_couk_new_csv's filter (line 353) to `if row.get('Season','').strip() not in season_labels: continue` where season_labels is a set/tuple instead of a single string. This keeps br.1/no.1/se.1/etc. (pure calendar-year, single label, unaffected) working unchanged while fixing ar.1's mixed-format seasons without touching Date parsing or risking double-counting from two differently-labelled torneos falling in the same nominal season.

all_findings.title: CALENDAR_YEAR_LEAGUES 'VERIFIED' comment is false for ar.1, and the guard test only covers cleanly-calendar br.1
all_findings.issue: The comment at lines 105-111 states the classification was 'VERIFIED per league by inspecting the feed's Season column (all of the new additions label seasons 2024/2025/2026, i.e. calendar-year)'. That is demonstrably false for ar.1, whose feed carries split-year labels like '2016/2017','2017/2018','2018/2019' (verified in data_cache/all_fdcouk_new_ar.1.csv). The only test guarding this logic, tests/test_csv_data_loader.py:84-89 (test_calendar_year_leagues_use_single_year), asserts _fd_couk_new_season_label only for br.1 and pl.1 — both cleanly-formatted — so the ar.1 mismatch produces zero matches while CI stays green. This false-confidence pattern is exactly how the codebase's recurring 'populated in training, degenerate at serve' bugs slipped through before.
all_findings.fix: Correct the comment to note ar.1's mixed split/calendar labels, and add a regression test that ar.1 actually loads >0 matches for 2016-17/2017-18/2018-19 (against a fixture reproducing the mixed Season column), plus a test that the calendar-year loader does not silently return [] for a season whose feed label is split-year.
all_findings.why_it_matters: An inaccurate 'verified' claim plus a test that only exercises the easy case means a real data-loss bug ships undetected and future edits can't rely on the guard.
all_findings.reason:
The core factual claim is confirmed but the "why it matters" consequence is not. Verified directly: awk over data_cache/all_fdcouk_new_ar.1.csv column 3 (Season) shows both split-year labels ("2012/2013","2013/2014","2016/2017","2017/2018","2018/2019","2019/2020") and calendar-year labels ("2014"..."2026") mixed in the same feed — so the comment at csv_data_loader.py:104-108 claiming this was "VERIFIED per league ... all of the new additions label seasons 2024/2025/2026, i.e. calendar-year" is false for ar.1. And tests/test_csv_data_loader.py:84-89 (TestNewLeaguesSeasonLabel.test_calendar_year_leagues_use_single_year) only asserts the label-format function for br.1, never ar.1, so this mismatch is indeed untested — that much is CONFIRMED.

However, the claimed consequence — "a real data-loss bug ships undetected" — does not hold. csv_data_loader.py:522-555 (load_season_league_data) tries FD_COUK_NEW second and explicitly guards against exactly this failure mode: `matches = parse_fd_couk_new_csv(...); if matches: return matches` (line 546) with the fallback comment "Nothing for this season in the new-leagues feed either — fall through to the stale-but-still-useful footballcsv mirror" (lines 548-549), then calls load_csv_from_cache_or_fetch (the footballcsv/cache.footballdata source, line 551), which does have an "ar.1" entry (LEAGUE_CODE_MAP:179, "ARG1"). This is proven empirically: data_cache/2016-17_ar.1.csv, 2012-13_ar.1.csv, and 2018-19_ar.1.csv all exist on disk with 300-450 rows each in the distinct footballcsv row shape ("Date,Team 1,FT,HT,Team 2" — confirmed by reading 2016-17_ar.1.csv:1-5), i.e. real match data for exactly the split-year seasons the FD_COUK_NEW feed silently zero-matches. So those seasons are not lost — they're transparently served by the footballcsv fallback, which is the very safety net the surrounding code comment (lines 106-108) describes.

Net: this is a real but low-impact documentation/test-coverage gap (the "VERIFIED" comment overclaims and the guard test has a blind spot), not the "silent data loss" bug the finding's severity/why_it_matters implies. Severity should be downgraded from medium to low, and the recommended fix should focus on correcting the comment and adding an ar.1 case to the label test — not "data loss" framing.
all_findings.corrected_fix: 1) Fix the comment at csv_data_loader.py:104-108 to state accurately that ar.1's own feed mixes split-year and calendar-year Season labels across its history (confirmed via data_cache/all_fdcouk_new_ar.1.csv), and that CALENDAR_YEAR_LEAGUES only needs to match the feed's *current/recent* convention for practical purposes because load_season_league_data already falls back to the footballcsv mirror when parse_fd_couk_new_csv returns zero matches (csv_data_loader.py:541-551). 2) Add a test asserting _fd_couk_new_season_label("2016-17", "ar.1") == "2017" (documenting the known, harmless mismatch against the feed's real "2016/2017" label for that era) alongside a test that load_season_league_data("2016-17", "ar.1") still returns non-empty matches (via the footballcsv fallback), so the fallback contract stays covered by CI rather than being an implicit, undocumented safety net.

all_findings.title: 'Colon Santa FE' vs 'Colon Santa Fe' in the ar.1 feed splits one club into two Elo/form identities
all_findings.issue: parse_fd_couk_new_csv() only .strip()s team names (line 358-360). The ar.1 new feed contains the same club under two casings, 'Colon Santa FE' and 'Colon Santa Fe' (verified: both appear as distinct Home values in all_fdcouk_new_ar.1.csv). Because team_stats / Elo / form are keyed by exact name, this one club accumulates two separate rating histories, each with half the matches and a degraded warm-up. (No other within-feed or cross-league name collisions were found, so the scope is this single club.)
all_findings.fix: Apply a generic normalization at parse time — case-fold plus collapse of internal whitespace — to team names before they become dict keys. This is deterministic string canonicalization, not fuzzy/similarity matching, so it does not violate the no-fuzzy-club-matching constraint, and it needs no per-club constant.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A split identity halves a club's rating sample and produces less reliable predictions for Colon home/away matches; small in isolation but the same class of degeneracy the audit is chasing.
all_findings.reason: csv_data_loader.py:357-358 only `.strip()`s home_team/away_team from the 'Home'/'Away' CSV columns — no case-folding or whitespace collapsing. The actual source file data_cache/all_fdcouk_new_ar.1.csv contains the same club under two distinct casings: \"Colon Santa FE\" (366 occurrences) and \"Colon Santa Fe\" (66 occurrences). Since team_stats/Elo/form dicts are keyed by the exact string, team_stats.json (lines 43232 and 46202) confirms two separate entries exist: \"Colon Santa Fe\" and \"Colon Santa FE\". A grep of the whole codebase shows no case-fold/normalize call anywhere in the csv_data_loader.py load path — the only normalization utilities that exist (club_mapping.py:146 `.lower()`, team_aliases.py:125 `strip_accents(...).lower()`) are not imported by csv_data_loader.py, so they never run during data loading/training. The finding is accurate as stated, including its severity (isolated to one club) and its proposed fix being deterministic canonicalization rather than fuzzy matching.
all_findings.corrected_fix: No correction needed to the substance; one implementation refinement: rather than writing new normalization logic inline, reuse the existing generic normalizer already in team_aliases.py (strip_accents + .lower(), plus collapsing internal whitespace with `' '.join(name.split())`) and apply it to home_team/away_team right after the .strip() calls at csv_data_loader.py:357-358, so the same canonicalization used elsewhere in the codebase is applied consistently at ingestion time before the names become dict keys.

all_findings.title: Tuned dc_rho is not threaded into the serving path (latent train/serve skew)
all_findings.issue: add_form_features accepts dc_rho and builds every training-row dc_* probability with it: data_processor.py:206 resolves dc_rho and :212 constructs DixonColesRatings(k=dc_k, rho=dc_rho), whose predict() passes self.rho into match_probabilities. The serving path does NOT: prepare_prediction_features at data_processor.py:728 calls dixon_coles.match_probabilities(...) with NO rho argument, so it always falls back to the module constant DC_RHO (dixon_coles.py:92, `DC_RHO if rho is None else rho`). This is asymmetric with dc_k, which is safe because its effect is baked into the persisted post-match ratings (home_dc_attack_post etc. carried through compute_team_stats), whereas rho is RE-APPLIED at prediction time from the module default. Today there is no numeric divergence only because every dc_rho in rating_constants_tuning.json equals the default -0.1 and production callers (csv_data_loader.py:667, main.py:80) pass no dc_rho. The instant rho is retuned, dc_home_prob/dc_draw_prob/dc_away_prob AND the derived dc_entropy/tightness diverge between training and serving — the exact 'feature populated in training, degenerate at prediction' bug class documented in HANDOFF.md. The alignment guard test cannot catch it because it drives both paths with the default rho.
all_findings.fix: Persist the trained dc_rho alongside the model (or on team_stats, like league_base_*_goals) and pass it as the rho argument at data_processor.py:728. Minimal alternative if rho is meant to stay fixed: stop advertising it as tunable and add an assert dc_rho == dixon_coles.DC_RHO so a future retune fails loudly instead of silently skewing.
all_findings.why_it_matters: It is a dormant instance of the codebase's single recurring bug (a feature trained on one value but served from another). It will not show up in tests and will silently degrade live predictions the first time rho is tuned.
all_findings.reason: data_processor.py:728-733 calls dixon_coles.match_probabilities() with only attack/defense/league-goals args, no rho — so it always falls through to dixon_coles.py:92 `DC_RHO if rho is None else rho`, using the hardcoded module constant -0.10. Meanwhile the training path (data_processor.py:181,206,212) explicitly resolves a tunable dc_rho parameter and constructs `DixonColesRatings(k=dc_k, rho=dc_rho)`, whose predict() at dixon_coles.py:119-124 passes `self.rho` (the tuned value) into match_probabilities. dc_k's tuning is safe because it only shapes the persisted post-match attack/defense ratings that flow through compute_team_stats onto team_stats and get read verbatim at serving time (dc_attack/dc_defense at line 729-730) — but rho is re-applied fresh at prediction time from the DC_RHO module constant, not from whatever was persisted/tuned during training. I verified rating_constants_tuning.json currently sets dc_rho: -0.1 in all 8 entries (matches DC_RHO default), and grepped csv_data_loader.py and main.py for dc_rho/dc_k — neither file passes dc_rho anywhere, confirming there is no current numeric skew, only a dormant one. This is exactly the same class of bug as the five documented incidents in HANDOFF.md: a training-tunable parameter that isn't threaded to the serving call.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is correct and doesn't need changes: persist the trained dc_rho (e.g. as a team_stats/league-level field similar to league_base_home_goals, or in the model bundle) and pass it explicitly as the rho argument at data_processor.py:728. The suggested cheap alternative — assert dc_rho == dixon_coles.DC_RHO whenever tuning runs, so a future retune fails loudly instead of silently skewing predictions — is also sound and lower-effort if rho tuning isn't actually needed per-league.

all_findings.title: Dixon-Coles tau goes negative for high expected-goal cells and the cell is silently zeroed
all_findings.issue: _tau returns `1 + lam_home*rho` for the (0,1) cell (dixon_coles.py:57) and `1 + lam_away*rho` for (1,0) (line 59). With rho = -0.10 these are negative once the relevant expected-goal rate exceeds 1/|rho| = 10. That is reachable: the per-league baseline (base_home_goals) is data-derived and can exceed the global 1.45 (a high-scoring league near ~2.0), and attack/defense are clipped up to DC_MAX=2.5, so exp_home = 2.0*2.5*2.5 = 12.5 gives tau(0,1) = 1 - 1.25 = -0.25. The resulting negative cell probability is clamped to 0 by `p = max(p, 0.0)` at line 93 and the grid is renormalized, so those scoreline cells are dropped from the distribution rather than correctly modeled — a small distortion of the H/D/A split for extreme mismatches, applied inconsistently only to the low-score cells.
all_findings.fix: Bound the low-score correction so it degrades gracefully instead of producing negative mass: inside _tau clamp the multiplier, e.g. use lam capped at 1/abs(rho) (or clamp the returned tau to a small positive floor), keeping the (0,1)/(1,0) adjustment non-negative for any reachable expected-goal rate.
all_findings.why_it_matters: For lopsided or high-scoring-league matchups the DC probabilities (a top model feature) are computed from a distribution missing its 1-0/0-1-style cells, biasing the very draw/low-score signal Dixon-Coles was added to capture.
all_findings.reason: dixon_coles.py:52-62 implements the standard Dixon-Coles tau exactly as in the 1997 paper: tau(0,1)=1+lam_home*rho, tau(1,0)=1+lam_away*rho (lines 57-59), with rho=DC_RHO=-0.10 (line 38). These two branches are the only ones that can go negative — tau(0,0)=1-lam_home*lam_away*rho is always >1 since rho<0, and tau(1,1)=1-rho=1.1 is constant. Negativity requires lam_home (or lam_away) > 1/|rho| = 10. Verified reachability: attack/defense multipliers are hard-clipped to [DC_MIN, DC_MAX]=[0.4, 2.5] in DixonColesRatings.update via _clip() (dixon_coles.py:42-43, 144-147), so the attack*defense product tops out at 2.5*2.5=6.25. exp_home = base_home_goals * home_attack * away_defense (line 74). base_home_goals is NOT a fixed constant at prediction/training time — data_processor.py:383-389 computes it per-competition as a rolling mean of goals-so-far (lg_hg/lg_n) once LEAGUE_BASELINE_MIN_MATCHES is reached, with no upper clamp. So exp_home = base_home_goals * 6.25 exceeds 10 whenever base_home_goals > 1.6, which is plausible for a genuinely high-scoring league/subset (the newly added leagues — MLS, JPN1, CHN1, ARG1 — widen the pool of per-league baselines and make an outlier more likely). When that happens, p at match_probabilities line 92 goes negative for the (0,1)/(1,0) cells and is clamped to 0.0 at line 93, then the grid is renormalized over the remaining mass — so those cells are silently dropped rather than correctly down-weighted, exactly as described. This is a real, if narrow-window, edge case in the tau formula's domain, not a misreading of the code.

all_findings.title: Season-gap Elo regression is applied only in training, never at serving — train/serve skew on the model's most important feature
all_findings.issue: In training (add_form_features, lines 395-396) a team idle more than ELO_SEASON_GAP (45) days has its Elo pulled 10% toward 1500 BEFORE that match's home_elo/elo_diff feature is computed: team_elo = 1500 + (elo-1500)*0.90. The serving path never does this. prepare_prediction_features reads home_elo = home.get('elo', ELO_START) (lines 670-671), and compute_team_stats sets that 'elo' straight from the last match's home_elo_post/away_elo_post (lines 878, 891) with no regression and no notion of a prediction date. So every prediction made across an off-season (which is the normal case — the app predicts arbitrary future/cross-league matchups against a dataset that ends at some past date) serves an un-regressed Elo. A team that finished a season at 1650 serves elo_diff built from 1650, whereas the training distribution for a post-gap match would have used 1500+150*0.90=1635 (and for an elite +300 side, a 30-point gap). This is exactly the recurring train/serve degeneracy this codebase has hit five times, now on elo_diff/abs_elo_diff/tightness — three features, one of which (elo_diff) is stated to be the model's single most important input. The guard test test_no_live_feature_is_wildly_outside_training_range (tests/test_data_processor.py:675-689) does NOT catch it: its fixture matches (self._built, lines 590-596) are all 8-20 days apart, so no >45-day gap is ever exercised, and the season-gap test at line 238 only checks the training side.
all_findings.fix: Make serving apply the same regression. Persist each team's last match date into team_stats in compute_team_stats (e.g. from the carried row date), give prepare_prediction_features an optional as_of_date (defaulting to the max date in the dataset), and before building elo_features compute: if _days_between(last_date, as_of) > ELO_SEASON_GAP: elo = ELO_START + (elo-ELO_START)*(1-ELO_SEASON_REGRESS). Then extend the guard fixture (or the season-gap test) to include a >45-day gap between two served matches so the alignment test actually exercises the regression path.
all_findings.why_it_matters: elo_diff is the model's top feature; a systematic magnitude bias on it at prediction time makes favourites look stronger than the model was trained to treat them after any off-season, the same silent-overconfidence failure documented in HANDOFF.md.
all_findings.reason: data_processor.py:392-396 shows training regresses a team's Elo toward 1500 by 10% (ELO_SEASON_REGRESS) whenever the gap since that team's last match exceeds ELO_SEASON_GAP (45 days), and this regressed value is what feeds home_elo/away_elo/elo_diff for that row. compute_team_stats (lines 878, 891) sets team_stats[team]['elo'] directly from row['home_elo_post']/row['away_elo_post'] of the most recent match, with no date captured alongside it and no regression applied. prepare_prediction_features (line 670-671) then reads home_elo = home.get('elo', ELO_START) verbatim — there is no as_of_date parameter, no last-match-date field in team_stats, and no gap check anywhere in the serving path. So any prediction made after a >45-day layoff (the normal case for an app predicting future/cross-league matchups against a historical dataset) serves an un-regressed Elo, producing a systematic distributional mismatch on elo_diff/abs_elo_diff/tightness relative to what the model was trained on for post-gap matches. This is the same class of train/serve skew documented five times in HANDOFF.md.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is correct in substance. Concretely: in compute_team_stats, capture each team's last match date (e.g. team_stats[team]['last_date'] = row.get('date')) alongside the elo/dc_attack/dc_defense block (lines 878/891 area). Give prepare_prediction_features an optional as_of_date (default: max date seen in the dataset, or datetime.now() if predicting genuinely future fixtures), and before building home_elo/away_elo apply the same rule used in training: if last_date and _days_between(last_date, as_of_date) > ELO_SEASON_GAP: elo = ELO_START + (elo - ELO_START) * (1 - ELO_SEASON_REGRESS) — reusing the same ELO_SEASON_GAP/ELO_SEASON_REGRESS constants (and _days_between helper) that add_form_features already uses, so the two paths can never drift apart on the threshold/factor. Then add a case to the existing guard test (or the season-gap test) with two served matches separated by >45 days to actually exercise this path — the current fixture (8-20 day gaps) can't catch a regression here.

all_findings.title: Home-advantage league scaling keys off total home scoring, not the home/away asymmetry it is meant to represent
all_findings.issue: The per-league home advantage is league_home_adv = elo_home_adv * (base_home_goals / LEAGUE_AVG_HOME_GOALS) (line 508). base_home_goals is the league's average HOME goals; dividing by the global home-goal baseline conflates 'this league is high-scoring overall' with 'this league has a large home advantage'. A high-scoring-both-ways league (home 1.8 / away 1.6, small real home edge) gets its home advantage scaled UP (1.8 > global ~1.5), while a low-scoring league with a genuinely large home edge (home 1.4 / away 0.9) gets scaled DOWN. The magnitude of home advantage is the home-vs-away asymmetry, which base_home_goals alone does not capture. This drives exp_home (line 509) and therefore every Elo update in that league, and it interacts with the 8 newly added leagues whose measured baselines only kick in after 200 matches (line 384).
all_findings.fix: Scale by the measured home/away asymmetry rather than absolute home scoring, e.g. league_home_adv = elo_home_adv * (base_home_goals / max(base_away_goals, 1e-6)) / (LEAGUE_AVG_HOME_GOALS / LEAGUE_AVG_AWAY_GOALS), so a league is boosted only when its home/away goal RATIO exceeds the global ratio. Keep the <200-match global-default fallback.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Systematically mis-sizes home advantage league by league, biasing the expected score (and thus every rating update) for high-scoring leagues, which now include several of the newly added competitions.
all_findings.reason: data_processor.py:508 computes league_home_adv = elo_home_adv * (base_home_goals / LEAGUE_AVG_HOME_GOALS) using only base_home_goals (line 385/388) against the global home-goal constant; base_away_goals (line 386/389) is computed but never used in this line. So the scaling reflects the league's absolute home-scoring level relative to the global average, not the home-vs-away asymmetry. A league that scores heavily both home and away (e.g. 1.8 home / 1.6 away) inflates league_home_adv purely because base_home_goals is high, even though its true home edge (the home-away gap) may be small; conversely a low-scoring league with a large home/away gap (1.4/0.9) gets its home-advantage scaling suppressed. This feeds exp_home at line 509 and therefore every Elo rating update for that league, including the 8 newly added leagues whose measured baselines only replace the global default after 200 matches (lines 384-389).
all_findings.corrected_fix:
At data_processor.py:508, replace with a ratio-of-ratios that measures the home/away asymmetry against the global asymmetry, keeping the existing <200-match fallback (base_home_goals/base_away_goals already default to the global constants at lines 388-389, so the ratio safely reduces to 1.0 in that case):
league_home_adv = elo_home_adv * ((base_home_goals / max(base_away_goals, 1e-6)) / (dixon_coles.LEAGUE_AVG_HOME_GOALS / max(dixon_coles.LEAGUE_AVG_AWAY_GOALS, 1e-6)))

all_findings.title: ELO_SEASON_GAP=45 days will misfire on mid-season data gaps, spuriously regressing ratings for the sparser newly-added leagues
all_findings.issue: The regression trigger is any team-level gap > ELO_SEASON_GAP=45 days (lines 68, 395-396), interpreted as 'off-season'. But it fires on ANY 45+ day hole in a team's fixture list, including missing-data gaps. With the working-tree changes extending history to 2012-13 and adding 8 leagues (NOR1/SWE1/FIN1/IRL1/MLS/JPN1/CHN1/ARG1) whose free-data coverage is thinner and less continuous than the big-5, incomplete fixture coverage for a team will look like an off-season and pull its Elo 10% toward 1500 mid-run. It can also fire multiple times for one team. The gap is measured from the team's true last recorded match (lines 354-355), so a coverage hole is indistinguishable from a real break.
all_findings.fix: Gate the regression on a genuine season boundary rather than a raw day-count — e.g. detect a change in the season/year field already available on the row, or require the gap to exceed a larger threshold (e.g. 60-75 days) that summer breaks clear but international breaks and short data holes do not; at minimum document that sparse-coverage leagues can trigger extra regressions and verify the added leagues have contiguous coverage.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Spurious regressions flatten Elo toward the mean for exactly the newly-added, less-battle-tested leagues, weakening elo_diff where the model has the least other signal.
all_findings.reason: The cited code is exactly as described. data_processor.py:392-396 iterates (home, away) with each team's last_date from team_overall_history (line 354-355, keyed only by team name across a team's entire history, not scoped per-league/competition), and regresses Elo toward ELO_START whenever _days_between(last_date, match_date) > ELO_SEASON_GAP (45, line 68) — a pure day-count gate with no season/competition-boundary check anywhere in the file (confirmed: no `season` field is read or used in data_processor.py at all). This is genuinely a data-coverage-sensitive trigger, and it is now exposed to the newly added leagues (csv_data_loader.py:89-101), which are all served from football-data.co.uk's "new" feed (one CSV per country since 2012-13, results-only). Several of these are plausibly irregular for reasons beyond ordinary summer breaks: ar.1 explicitly \"pools Liga Profesional + Copa de la Liga\" (csv_data_loader.py:100), i.e. two separate competitions concatenated into one series per team, which is exactly the kind of structure that can produce a >45-day hole between a team's last match in one competition and its next in the other; cn.1 (Chinese Super League) and others have historically had irregular mid-season stoppages. However, I did not empirically verify actual date gaps in the ingested CSVs (would require pulling the feed and checking per-team gap distributions), so I cannot confirm this actually fires spuriously in practice versus just tracking genuine season boundaries cleanly. The mechanism and exposure are real; the claimed harm is plausible but unverified against real gap data, and the underlying ELO_SEASON_GAP=45 threshold/regression mechanism is pre-existing (not itself part of the new diff) — only the leagues newly exposed to it are new. Severity=low is fair.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix (gate on season/year field) requires plumbing a `season` value into data_processor rows, which csv_data_loader.py already has available (AVAILABLE_SEASONS / _fd_couk_new_season_label) but currently does not pass through to add_form_features. A cheaper interim fix matching the existing no-lookahead style: raise ELO_SEASON_GAP for calendar-year/thin-coverage leagues specifically (e.g. keep 45 for Aug-May leagues but use ~75-90 days for the CALENDAR_YEAR_LEAGUES set already defined in csv_data_loader.py:109-111, since that set already flags exactly the leagues at risk), or pass `competition` alongside last_date so the gap is measured per-(team, competition) instead of per-team-globally, avoiding cross-competition concatenation gaps like ar.1's pooled feed.

all_findings.title: Calibrator is fit on in-sample predictions (final pipeline was refit on ALL data first)
all_findings.issue: _fit_sklearn refits the shipped pipeline on the FULL dataset at line 687 (`pipe.fit(X_arr, y_arr, ...)`) with no tail excluded. train(calibrate=True) then calls fit_calibration on X[cal_lo:cal_hi] (line 989), a slice of that same data the pipeline has already trained on. fit_calibration (line 1157) does `raw = self.pipeline.predict_proba(X_holdout)` on those in-sample rows, so the recalibration map is learned against IN-SAMPLE probabilities, which are systematically less overconfident than the out-of-sample probabilities the model actually emits in production. The calibrator therefore under-corrects overconfidence for real (unseen) matches — the reworked calibration is being validated and fit on data that does not represent serving conditions. The comment at line 724-725 calls this an 'untouched holdout … never seen', which is false: the CV folds are purged, but the final refit at line 687 saw every row.
all_findings.fix: Exclude the tail holdout from the final refit, OR generate the calibration targets out-of-sample. Concretely: reserve the last HOLDOUT_FRACTION of X for calibration/eval only, refit `pipe` on X_arr[:-n_hold] (still the ship-time pipeline), and fit_calibration on the reserved slice; or compute the calibration `raw` via sklearn `cross_val_predict` so the probabilities the calibrator sees are genuinely out-of-fold.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The entire point of the reworked calibration is to make displayed probabilities mean what they say on live matches; fitting it on in-sample predictions defeats that and reproduces exactly the class of 'trained-vs-served mismatch' bug this codebase keeps hitting.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:966 calls self._fit_sklearn(X, y, ...) passing the FULL X/y (train()'s own parameters, no tail already withheld). Inside _fit_sklearn, line 687 does pipe.fit(X_arr, y_arr, clf__sample_weight=sw_full) — a fit on the entire dataset, X_arr/y_arr being the same full arrays converted from X, y via _to_numpy at line 581. self.pipeline is set to this pipe at line 691. Back in train(), lines 983-989 then slice cal_lo:cal_hi from the same X/y and call self.fit_calibration(X[cal_lo:cal_hi], y[cal_lo:cal_hi]). fit_calibration (line 1157) does raw = self.pipeline.predict_proba(X_holdout) — i.e., predict_proba on rows the pipeline was already fit on at line 687. So the calibrator's raw probabilities are in-sample, not out-of-fold. The comment at 724-725 ('genuine, untouched holdout ... never seen during CV-fold fitting order-wise') describes the *evaluation* holdout used for self._compute_prob_metrics (also computed via pipe.predict_proba(Xte) at line 734, same leakage) — it does not claim protection from the final full-data refit, and the comment at 979-982 similarly only claims separation between the calibration-fit half and the score-only half (cal vs test), not separation from the training set. Neither holdout slice is excluded from the line-687 refit. This is a real train/calibrate-on-in-sample-predictions leakage bug, consistent with this codebase's documented recurring pattern of serving-time/eval-time data not matching what was actually trained on.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is directionally correct and sufficiently concrete; two refinements: (1) since _fit_sklearn already computes an evaluation holdout internally (test_size = last 20% of n, lines 727-732) for _compute_prob_metrics, that internal holdout has the identical leakage (pipe.predict_proba(Xte) on line 734 where Xte was part of the line-687 refit) — fixing calibration alone without also fixing _compute_prob_metrics leaves the reported log-loss/Brier/RPS metrics equally in-sample-contaminated, so both should be fixed together, not just the calibrator. (2) Concretely: pass a held-out fraction (e.g. the same calibrate_frac tail) into _fit_sklearn/train, fit the final pipe.fit at line 687 on X_arr[:-n_hold]/y_arr[:-n_hold] only, and use the withheld X_arr[-n_hold:] tail (split further into cal/test as train() already does at lines 985-987) for both the holdout metrics currently computed at lines 727-736 and for fit_calibration. This keeps the single-refit-then-calibrate architecture but makes both the reported metrics and the calibrator genuinely out-of-sample, matching the "untouched holdout" claim the comments already assert.

all_findings.title: Saved rps/log_loss/brier are UNCALIBRATED but the model ships calibrated probabilities
all_findings.issue: _compute_prob_metrics (called at line 735) scores `proba = pipe.predict_proba(Xte)` — the RAW pipeline output — and stores it as self.log_loss_/brier_/rps_ (lines 762-766). These run inside _fit_sklearn, which returns BEFORE train() ever calls fit_calibration (line 989). So the calibrator is None when the metrics are computed. But at serve time predict() (line 1048) and evaluate.py (line 257) both route through apply_calibration, so users see CALIBRATED probabilities. The rps/log_loss/brier persisted to model.json (save lines 1199-1201, 1214-1215) and returned by get_metrics therefore describe probabilities no user ever sees, and cannot be compared against the ~0.19-0.21 RPS ceiling the comments invoke. When calibrate=True (the shipped configuration per HANDOFF/main.py), the reported and shipped numbers diverge.
all_findings.fix: After fit_calibration runs in train(), recompute the holdout prob-metrics through apply_calibration on the (out-of-sample) holdout, e.g. `self._compute_prob_metrics(yte, self.apply_calibration(pipe.predict_proba(Xte)))`, and store those. Alternatively label the stored fields explicitly as pre-calibration and add calibrated counterparts.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The metrics are the primary evidence the calibration rework improved anything; if they grade the uncalibrated model, every calibration decision (C, prior-blend, RPS-vs-ceiling comparison) is being made on the wrong numbers.
all_findings.reason: Verified the full sequence in model_trainer.py. In `_fit_sklearn` (called at model_trainer.py:966 from `train()`), the holdout metrics are computed at lines 733-735: `proba = pipe.predict_proba(Xte)` (raw pipeline output, no calibrator involved) → `self._compute_prob_metrics(yte, proba)`, which sets `self.log_loss_`, `self.brier_`, `self.rps_` (lines 762-766). `_fit_sklearn` returns at line 742, back into `train()`. Only *after* that return does `train()` reach the calibration block at lines 983-989: `if calibrate and self.pipeline is not None: ... self.fit_calibration(X[cal_lo:cal_hi], y[cal_lo:cal_hi])`. Nothing after `fit_calibration` recomputes or overwrites `self.log_loss_/brier_/rps_` — `train()` proceeds straight to `self.trained_at = ...` and `return self.get_metrics()` (lines 991-992), which just rounds and returns the already-set (pre-calibration) values (lines 1014-1019). Meanwhile `predict()` (line 1041-1048) explicitly calls `self.apply_calibration(...)` on the pipeline's raw proba before returning results to users, and `evaluate.py:257` does the same (`model.apply_calibration(model.pipeline.predict_proba(Xte))`). So the persisted/reported log_loss/brier/rps describe uncalibrated probabilities while every consumer-facing path (predict, evaluate) uses calibrated ones — exactly the mismatch described. One additional wrinkle worth noting for the fix: `_fit_sklearn`'s metrics holdout is the last `int(n*0.2)` rows (line 727), and `calibrate_frac` defaults to the same 0.2, so with defaults the calibration-fit slice (`cal_lo:cal_hi`, first part of the last 20%) overlaps/is nested inside the exact rows already used for the stored metrics — so a naive "just recompute after calibration on Xte/yte" fix would partially grade the calibrator on its own fitting data, unless it's restricted to the same second-half slice evaluate.py uses (lines 246-257 comments already describe that split).
all_findings.corrected_fix: In `train()`, after the `if calibrate and self.pipeline is not None: ...` block finishes fitting the calibrator, recompute and overwrite the stored metrics using the calibrated probabilities — but score on the disjoint second-half slice (the same `n_test` tail slice evaluate.py uses), not on the calibrator's own fitting slice, to avoid grading the calibrator on its own data. E.g. reuse the `cal_hi:` (or equivalent held-out test tail) rows: `Xte2, yte2 = X[cal_hi:], y[cal_hi:]` (or explicitly store the Xte/yte from `_fit_sklearn` and slice out the calibration-fit rows), then `self._compute_prob_metrics(yte2, self.apply_calibration(self.pipeline.predict_proba(Xte2)))`. Alternatively, keep both: rename the current fields to `log_loss_raw_`/`brier_raw_`/`rps_raw_` and add calibrated counterparts so both pre- and post-calibration numbers are visible and neither silently mislabels the other.

all_findings.title: apply_calibration clips inputs unconditionally — mismatched for a calibrator fit before the clip existed
all_findings.issue: apply_calibration always transforms inputs through _calib_logspace, which clips proba to [0.01,0.99] (lines 1112-1114) before the log. A calibrator (LogisticRegression) persisted by an older build was fit on UNCLIPPED log-probabilities (the clip is new to this rework). load() (line 1304) restores that old calibrator object verbatim, and apply_calibration then feeds it clipped-and-logged inputs it was never trained on — a train/serve skew on the exact tail region (very confident predictions) the clip was added to tame. There is no version guard tying the clip to the calibrator that was fit with it; the joblib and the CALIB_CLIP_LO/HI constants can drift independently.
all_findings.fix: Persist a calibrator-schema marker (e.g. a `calib_clip=[lo,hi]` field written alongside calib_C in save() and read in load()), and in _calib_logspace use the loaded bounds; when the marker is absent (old calibrator), skip the clip so the transform matches how that calibrator was fit. Bump MODEL_VERSION when the calibration input transform changes.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A silently mismatched input transform on old models produces confidently wrong probabilities with no error — the recurring failure mode this codebase is auditing for.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:1108-1114 clips inputs to [0.01, 0.99] before the log — this bound is new. Diffing against the last commit (`git show HEAD:model_trainer.py`, old `apply_calibration`/`fit_calibration` around lines 980-1007) shows the previous transform was `np.log(np.clip(proba, 1e-9, 1.0))`, i.e. an effectively-unclipped log. So a calibrator (LogisticRegression) fit under the old code learned coefficients over a materially different input range in the confident tails (e.g. raw proba 0.001 -> old logp ≈ -6.9 vs new logp ≈ -4.6). `load()` (line 1304) restores `self.calibrator` from `model.calib.joblib` with no check against `self.version`/clip bounds, and `apply_calibration` (line 1116-1121) unconditionally runs the new `_calib_logspace` clip on whatever calibrator was loaded. There is genuinely no version guard anywhere in the file — grepping for `self.version` shows it's read at load (line 1252) and written at save, but never compared or used to gate calibrator behavior. This is not just theoretical: in the current working tree, `model.joblib` is modified (mid-retrain, git status shows `M`) while `model.calib.joblib` and `model.json` are byte-identical to HEAD (`git diff --stat -- model.json` empty, and HEAD's model.json already shows `calib_C: None`/`calib_shrinkage: None` even at trained_at 2026-07-27T01:04), confirming the pipeline and the calibrator artifact are two independently-saved files with no cross-check binding them together.
all_findings.corrected_fix: Add a `calib_clip: [CALIB_CLIP_LO, CALIB_CLIP_HI]` field written in save() next to calib_C/calib_shrinkage, and in load() store it as `self.calib_clip_ = data.get("calib_clip")`. Have `_calib_logspace` use `self.calib_clip_` if set, falling back to the class constants only when absent (i.e. no clip/1e-9 clip for calibrators saved before this field existed, matching how they were actually fit) — this makes the transform self-describing per artifact instead of relying on a MODEL_VERSION bump, which is easy to forget to do in lockstep with a clip-constant edit (as happened here: MODEL_VERSION is still "3.0.0" despite the clip changing).

all_findings.title: Inner-split selects (C, prior-blend w) against a 70%-fit base and 70% prior, but deploys a 100%-refit calibrator with the full-holdout prior
all_findings.issue: The inner-split loop (lines 1166-1176) fits candidate calibrators on logp[:cut] (first 70%) and computes the blend prior from y_arr[:cut] (line 1170), scoring log-loss on the last 30% to pick (C, w). But the SHIPPED calibrator is refit on the full holdout (line 1179) and class_prior_ is recomputed over the FULL holdout (line 1180). So the (C, w) chosen as best were validated against a different base map AND a different prior vector than the ones actually used at apply time. The blend weight w in particular was tuned to correct a 70%-fit map's residual, not the 100%-fit map's, so its selected value is only approximately right for what deploys.
all_findings.fix: After refitting the final calibrator on the full holdout, either keep the selection base consistent (select on the same 100%-fit map via an inner CV rather than a single 70/30 split), or at minimum recompute the inner-split prior from the same subset the base was fit on AND re-verify the chosen w against the deployed calibrator's outputs before storing it.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The rework's headline improvement is that C and the prior-blend are 'selected by log-loss, not hand-picked'; if the selection target differs from the deployed object, the selection is weaker than claimed and can pick a w that is not actually log-loss-optimal for the shipped map.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:1166-1180 confirms the finding exactly. The inner-selection loop (1166-1176) fits `clf = LogisticRegression(C=C).fit(logp[:cut], y_arr[:cut])` (70% split), computes `prior` from `y_arr[:cut]` (line 1170, the 70% slice), and blends/scores against `logp[cut:]`/`y_arr[cut:]` (the 30% holdout) to pick best (C, w) by log-loss. But the shipped calibrator at line 1179 is `LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=2000).fit(logp, y_arr)` — refit on the FULL holdout (100%, not the 70% cut) — and `self.class_prior_` at line 1180 is `[(y_arr == c).mean() ...]`, i.e. the full-holdout empirical prior, not the 70%-slice prior used during selection. So the (C, w) pair was validated against a base map trained on 70% of the data blended with the 70%-slice prior, then deployed with a base map trained on 100% of the data blended with the 100%-slice prior — two different objects. The mismatch is real but likely small in practice since C only controls L2 strength (not wildly sensitive to n going from 0.7N to N) and the two priors are estimates of the same underlying distribution from overlapping samples, so w's optimality is only approximately preserved, not exactly broken.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is reasonable; a lighter-weight alternative worth adding: keep the 70/30 split for selecting C, but when computing `prior` for scoring at line 1170 either (a) use the full-holdout prior (y_arr, not y_arr[:cut]) even during selection so the prior term is consistent between selection and deployment, or (b) after picking (C, w) via the current 70/30 procedure, do a final sanity check comparing log-loss of the deployed (100%-fit, full-prior) calibrator against the discarded alternative (w=0 i.e. no blend) on the 30% holdout to confirm w still helps before shipping it — cheap and catches cases where the selection would have picked a different w had it seen the deployed prior.

all_findings.title: calib_shrinkage_ None-fallback applies a 0.06 prior blend a calibrator may never have been fit/selected with
all_findings.issue: apply_calibration reads calib_shrinkage_ and, when it is None, falls back to CALIBRATION_SHRINKAGE=0.06 (lines 1124-1126), then blends in class_prior_ if that is non-None (line 1127). A model persisted at an intermediate version that saved class_prior but not calib_shrinkage (load() line 1275 → None) would get a 0.06 prior blend injected at serve time even though its calibrator was selected/fit under a possibly-different or zero blend. The guard `prior is not None and w>0` means this only bites when class_prior_ survives round-trip but calib_shrinkage_ does not, so it is narrow, but the silent injection of an unselected blend weight is still a correctness gap.
all_findings.fix: Make the fallback explicit and safe: if calib_shrinkage_ is None, treat w as 0.0 (no blend) rather than 0.06, so a model that never recorded a blend weight is served with no blend instead of a guessed one. Reserve CALIBRATION_SHRINKAGE strictly for the fit-time selection fallback (line 1177), not the apply-time path.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Serving a prior-blend weight that was never validated for that calibrator shifts every displayed probability toward the base rate by an unaudited amount.
all_findings.reason:
Verified directly against the code and the actual shipped artifact. model_trainer.py:1210-1211 shows `class_prior` and `calib_shrinkage` are written together in save(), and fit_calibration() (lines 1180/1182) always sets `self.class_prior_` and `self.calib_shrinkage_` in the same call — so within one code version they can never diverge. The divergence the finding describes requires a model.json written by an older save() that predates the `calib_shrinkage` key.

That is not hypothetical: I inspected the repo's actual checked-in model.json and confirmed the key is genuinely absent (`"calib_shrinkage" in d` → False) while `class_prior` is present (`[0.3067, 0.2571, 0.4362]`). So load() at model_trainer.py:1274-1275 sets `self.class_prior_` to that 3-vector and `self.calib_shrinkage_` to None (from `data.get("calib_shrinkage")` on a missing key). Then apply_calibration (lines 1123-1129) hits `w is None → w = self.CALIBRATION_SHRINKAGE (0.06)` and blends every served probability vector 94/6 with that stale prior — a blend weight this particular calibrator was never fit or selected with (whatever w the original fit_calibration() picked from {0.0, 0.03, 0.06, 0.10} was simply never persisted). This is live in the currently shipped model, not just a theoretical backward-compat edge case, which arguably raises the real-world severity above "low."
all_findings.corrected_fix:
In apply_calibration (model_trainer.py:1123-1126), change the None-fallback to 0.0, not CALIBRATION_SHRINKAGE:
```
w = getattr(self, "calib_shrinkage_", None)
if w is None:
    w = 0.0  # unknown blend weight for this calibrator -> no blend, not a guess
```
Reserve CALIBRATION_SHRINKAGE (0.06) strictly for the fit-time fallback at line 1177 when the inner split is too small to select a value at training time. Separately, the currently shipped model.json/model.joblib is running with this exact stale state right now — retraining/resaving once (so calib_shrinkage is persisted) or shipping this fix will both fix it; the fix alone corrects behavior even without retraining.

all_findings.title: Persisted/dashboard RPS, log-loss and Brier are computed on RAW (uncalibrated) probabilities, so they describe numbers no user ever sees and disagree with evaluation.json
all_findings.issue: self.rps_, self.log_loss_ and self.brier_ are set by _compute_prob_metrics(yte, proba) where proba = pipe.predict_proba(Xte) is the RAW pipeline output (model_trainer.py:734).
