This runs inside _fit_sklearn, BEFORE calibration is fitted (fit_calibration is only called afterwards in train() at line 989), and the metrics are never recomputed on calibrated probabilities. Yet the shipped prediction path always applies calibration (predict at model_trainer.py:1047-1048), and evaluate.py deliberately reports RPS on CALIBRATED proba (model.apply_calibration(...) at evaluate.py:257, fed to _rps at evaluate.py:283) precisely because raw numbers 'report numbers no user ever sees' (evaluate.py:256). The result: the model.joblib 'rps' field / get_metrics()['rps'] (surfaced to the dashboard at model_trainer.py:1018 and saved at 1200) is a RAW score, while evaluation.json's 'rps' is a CALIBRATED score. Two different numbers under the same name, and the get_metrics comment (model_trainer.py:1016) invites comparing the raw number to the ~0.19-0.21 calibrated SOTA ceiling — apples to oranges. Whether calibration helped or hurt RPS is invisible in the persisted metric.
all_findings.fix: After fit_calibration() succeeds in train() (model_trainer.py:989), recompute the probabilistic metrics on calibrated probabilities so the saved rps_/log_loss_/brier_ match what users see: call self._compute_prob_metrics(y_slice, self.apply_calibration(self.pipeline.predict_proba(X_slice))) on the held-out slice. Use the SECOND half of the tail holdout (indices cal_hi:n, the same slice evaluate.py scores) — never the first half, which the calibrator was just fit on. Alternatively keep the raw value but rename it (e.g. rps_raw_) and add a separate calibrated rps so the two are not conflated.
all_findings.why_it_matters: RPS/log-loss are stated to be the primary metrics that 'move when calibration improves' (evaluate.py:278-282); reporting them pre-calibration hides exactly the effect the recent calibration rework was meant to demonstrate and makes the dashboard number non-comparable to both the literature ceiling and evaluation.json.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:734-735 sets proba = pipe.predict_proba(Xte) (raw, uncalibrated pipeline output) inside _fit_sklearn, and _compute_prob_metrics (744-766) sets self.log_loss_, self.brier_, self.rps_ from that raw proba. This runs before calibration exists: train() only calls self.fit_calibration(...) later, at line 989, and nothing after that recomputes/overwrites log_loss_/brier_/rps_ on calibrated probabilities. get_metrics() (994-1019) simply rounds and returns the stale raw self.rps_/log_loss_/brier_, and these are what's saved (to_dict at ~1198-1200) and reloaded (from_dict at ~1263-1265), i.e. what ships in model.joblib and reaches the dashboard. By contrast evaluate.py:257 explicitly computes proba = model.apply_calibration(model.pipeline.predict_proba(Xte)) — calibrated — before calling _rps/_log_loss (line 283), and the code's own comment at evaluate.py:256 states this is deliberate so the report reflects what users actually see. Since the live prediction path (model_trainer.py:1047-1048) always applies calibration, the persisted/dashboard rps_/log_loss_/brier_ are computed on probabilities nobody is ever served, while evaluation.json's same-named metrics are computed on the calibrated probabilities that are actually served. This is exactly the discrepancy described in the finding.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is correct in spirit and should be applied essentially as stated: after self.fit_calibration(X[cal_lo:cal_hi], y[cal_lo:cal_hi]) succeeds at model_trainer.py:989, recompute self.log_loss_/self.brier_/self.rps_ on calibrated probabilities using the SAME holdout tail that _fit_sklearn already reserved (X_arr[-test_size:]/y_arr[-test_size:] at lines 730-731), not the calibration-fit slice (cal_lo:cal_hi) or its cal_hi:n remainder computed inside train() only for calibrate_frac — to keep semantics aligned with the existing self.test_samples/holdout size, call something like: proba_cal = self.apply_calibration(self.pipeline.predict_proba(Xte_holdout)); self._compute_prob_metrics(yte_holdout, proba_cal), guarding with try/except mirroring the existing pattern at 736-740. Xte_holdout/yte_holdout must be threaded out of _fit_sklearn (or recomputed identically from X/y using the same n/test_size formula) since they're currently local to that method. The alternative suggested (rename to rps_raw_ and add a separate calibrated field) is also acceptable and arguably safer since it preserves the raw diagnostic while adding the calibrated one that dashboard/get_metrics should surface as the primary "rps".

all_findings.title: The raw-proba metric holdout is the same last-20% slice the calibrator is later fit on, so any in-place calibration fix must score on the non-overlapping second half
all_findings.issue: _compute_prob_metrics is fed Xte = X_arr[-test_size:] with test_size = 20% of n (model_trainer.py:727-731). train() then fits the calibrator on X[cal_lo:cal_hi] = the FIRST HALF of that same last-20% window (cal_lo,cal_hi computed at model_trainer.py:985-987). Today this is only latent because the metric uses raw proba, but it becomes an active correctness bug the moment someone applies the fix in finding #1 naively over the whole 20% slice: half those matches are the calibrator's own fitting data, which grades the calibrator on data it saw and reproduces the exact selection bias evaluate.py:247-251 was written to avoid.
all_findings.fix: When recomputing calibrated metrics, restrict scoring to X_arr[cal_hi:] (the second half of the tail holdout, i.e. n_test = n_hold - n_hold//2 matches) so the metric holdout and the calibration-fit set are disjoint, mirroring evaluate.py's half/n_test split at evaluate.py:250-252.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Without this, the corrected calibrated RPS would be optimistically biased and would not match evaluation.json, defeating the purpose of computing it.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:730 sets Xte = X_arr[-test_size:] with test_size = int(n*0.2) (line 727), which equals the full n_hold window used for calibration (calibrate_frac defaults to 0.2 at line 944). fit_calibration is fit on X[cal_lo:cal_hi] where cal_lo, cal_hi = n-n_hold, n-n_test (lines 985-989) — i.e. exactly the first half of that same Xte window. evaluate.py:245-252 explicitly avoids this by scoring only X[-n_test:] (the second, disjoint half), with a comment stating scoring the whole slice would 'quietly grade the calibrator on its own fitting data.' Currently _compute_prob_metrics (line 744) only receives raw, uncalibrated pipe.predict_proba(Xte) (line 734), so the leakage is inert today — but any change that makes this path score calibrated probabilities over the same Xte would reproduce the exact bias evaluate.py was written to avoid, and would diverge from evaluation.json's numbers.
all_findings.corrected_fix: When adding/using calibrated metrics from train(), restrict the scoring slice to the second half only: n_hold = max(int(n*calibrate_frac),1); half = n_hold // 2; n_test = n_hold - half; Xte, yte = X_arr[-n_test:], y_arr[-n_test:] — mirroring evaluate.py:245-252 exactly (do not reuse test_size = int(n*0.2) computed independently at line 727, since it must track calibrate_frac, not a hardcoded 0.2, to stay consistent if calibrate_frac is ever changed).

all_findings.title: _rps is duplicated verbatim in two files; identical today but exactly the kind of two-path code the codebase has repeatedly seen drift
all_findings.issue: _rps in evaluate.py:59-71 and model_trainer.py:461-478 are byte-for-byte identical in logic (same cumsum, same [:-1] drop, same /(P.shape[1]-1) normalization) and both correctly assume ascending ordinal classes. But they are two independent copies. Given this project's documented recurring failure mode (five features that silently diverged between training and serving paths), keeping the scoring rule itself forked invites a future edit to one copy — e.g. a clip or a class-order change — that silently makes the training-side rps_ and the evaluation-side rps incomparable.
all_findings.fix: Delete evaluate.py's copy and import the single implementation: 'from model_trainer import _rps' (evaluate.py already imports MatchPredictorModel from model_trainer at line 231). Do the same for _log_loss vs model_trainer._logloss_proba, which are also near-duplicates.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A single shared scoring function guarantees the dashboard number and evaluation.json number are computed the same way and cannot drift, which is the whole basis for comparing them.
all_findings.reason: evaluate.py:59-71 and model_trainer.py:461-478 are identical in logic (same asarray/cumsum/[:-1] slice/normalization by P.shape[1]-1). evaluate.py already does `from model_trainer import MatchPredictorModel` at line 231, so importing `_rps` from the same module is a zero-cost, low-risk fix — no new dependency, no circular-import risk since evaluate.py already depends on model_trainer. The maintainability risk described (one copy edited, e.g. clip added or class order changed, silently making training-side and eval-side RPS incomparable) is a real and accurate characterization of this codebase's documented failure pattern.
all_findings.corrected_fix: Fix as proposed is correct: replace evaluate.py's local `_rps` def with `from model_trainer import _rps` (evaluate.py:231 already imports from model_trainer, confirming no circular-import issue). For `_log_loss`, note model_trainer's closest counterpart is `_logloss_proba` (a staticmethod at model_trainer.py:1133, likely nested inside a class) rather than a free function — either promote it to a module-level function importable by evaluate.py, or leave `_log_loss` as evaluate.py's own copy if the staticmethod isn't easily reusable without refactoring; don't claim it's a one-line import without checking that method's binding first.

all_findings.title: Recency scaling + global renormalization silently undoes the balanced class-weight correction
all_findings.issue: In both the CV folds (lines 406-410) and the final refit (lines 681-685) the code does sw = compute_sample_weight("balanced", ytr); sw = sw * rw; sw = sw * (len(sw)/sw.sum()). compute_sample_weight("balanced") deliberately gives every class an EQUAL total weight (each class sums to n/n_classes) to rescue the draw-minority class. Multiplying by the recency vector rw scales each class total by that class's MEAN recency weight, and the final sw*(len/sum) is a single global scalar that only restores the grand total to ~n — it does NOT re-equalize the per-class totals. So whenever the class mix differs across time (it does here: 8 leagues were only added for recent seasons, and draw rates vary by era/league), recency weighting reweights the classes as a side effect. If draws are even slightly older-skewed, their aggregate weight drops and the balanced draw-recall correction the whole scheme exists for is quietly weakened — exactly the class the model already struggles with.
all_findings.fix: Renormalize PER CLASS instead of globally: after sw = sw * rw, for each class c rescale sw[ytr==c] so its sum equals the pre-recency balanced total for that class (n/n_classes). That keeps every class's aggregate influence identical to the balanced scheme while still letting recency redistribute weight WITHIN each class. Apply the same per-class renorm in the refit block at lines 681-685.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The balanced weights are the mechanism that keeps the model from ignoring draws to chase accuracy; recency weighting can partially cancel it without any visible signal, degrading the very metric (draw recall / RPS) recency was added to improve.
all_findings.reason: Read model_trainer.py:397-410 (CV folds) and 678-689 (final refit). `compute_sample_weight("balanced", ytr)` assigns each sample in class c weight n/(n_classes*n_c), so summed per class the total is exactly n/n_classes for every class — that's the whole point of "balanced". After `sw = sw * rw` (line 409 / 684), the per-class total becomes (n/n_classes) * mean(rw restricted to that class), i.e. it now depends on that class's average recency weight. The final line `sw = sw * (len(sw)/sw.sum())` (line 410 / 685) is a single scalar applied identically to every sample, so it rescales the grand total back to ~n but cannot restore per-class equality — the relative skew between classes (proportional to each class's mean recency weight) survives unchanged. So if draws (or any class) skew toward older matches on average — plausible here since 8 new leagues (NOR1/SWE1/FIN1/IRL1/MLS/JPN1/CHN1/ARG1, per csv_data_loader.py) only contribute recent-era rows and per-league/era draw rates differ — the balanced correction for that class is silently diluted after recency weighting is layered on. The bug is present identically in both the CV-fold path (410) and the final-refit path (685), consistent with the finding.
all_findings.corrected_fix: In both spots, after `sw = sw * rw`, renormalize within each class rather than globally: for each class c, scale sw[ytr==c] (or sw_full[y_arr==c]) so it sums to n/n_classes (the same total the pure "balanced" weighting would have given that class) — e.g. `for c in classes: mask = (ytr==c); sw[mask] *= (n/len(classes)) / sw[mask].sum()`. This keeps every class's aggregate influence pinned to the balanced target while still letting recency reweight samples within each class, and the grand total will automatically be ~n (sum of n/n_classes over all classes), so the extra global `sw*(len/sum)` scalar becomes unnecessary. Apply the same change at both line ~410 and ~685.

all_findings.title: Recency weights are not applied during the hyperparameter / select_k / voting-weight search
all_findings.issue: The tuning searches all route through _select_best -> _evaluate_pipeline (called at line 367) which is invoked WITHOUT the recency_weights argument, so it defaults to None. Only the final full-data evaluate (line 675-676) and refit (line 682-685) use recency. This means select_k, the rf/histgb/lr params, and the voting weights are all chosen under an unweighted regime and then the model is fit under a weighted one. The chosen config is not necessarily the one that is best for the weighting the shipped model actually uses. (Secondary: the tuning subsample is Xt = X_arr[-tuning_cap:], so even a fix must slice recency_weights[-tuning_cap:] to stay index-aligned.)
all_findings.fix: Thread recency_weights through _select_best/build_fn into the tuning _evaluate_pipeline calls (slicing to the tuning subsample: recency_weights[-tuning_cap:] when the cap is applied), so config selection and final fit share the same sample-weighting regime.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Selecting hyperparameters and combiner weights under a different sample-weighting scheme than the final fit means the 'winning' config is chosen for the wrong objective; the benefit of recency weighting can be masked or reversed by a mis-selected config.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:358-371 defines _select_best, which calls _evaluate_pipeline(pipe, X, y, n_folds=n_folds, purge_gap=purge_gap) at line 367 — no recency_weights kwarg is passed, so it takes the default None from _evaluate_pipeline's signature (line 374-375, applied only if not None at line 407-410). Every tuning call in _fit_sklearn (select_k at 619-622, rf/histgb/lr grids at 631-634 and 640-651, voting weights at 659-663) goes through _select_best on the Xt/yt subsample defined at 599-603 (Xt, yt = X_arr[-tuning_cap:], y_arr[-tuning_cap:] when len(X_arr) > tuning_cap=8000), all unweighted by recency. Only the post-tuning _evaluate_pipeline call at 675-676 and the final refit's sample-weight construction at 681-685 actually multiply in recency_weights. So hyperparameters/select_k/voting weights are chosen under a plain-balanced-weight regime while the shipped pipeline is fit (and reported-scored) under a recency-weighted regime — a real train/tune inconsistency, not a false alarm. The secondary index-alignment point also holds: recency_weights is parallel to the full X_arr (built from sample_dates in train(), lines ~955), so any fix that reuses it inside the Xt/yt-based tuning loop must also slice recency_weights[-tuning_cap:] when the cap is applied, or indices will desync between the weight array and the tuning subsample.
all_findings.corrected_fix: Thread an optional recency_weights parameter through _select_best (add a rw=None kwarg, slice it inside using the same tr indices as X/y before passing to _evaluate_pipeline) and through the lambda build_fn calls' surrounding scope in _fit_sklearn. Concretely: compute rwt = recency_weights[-tuning_cap:] if len(X_arr) > tuning_cap else recency_weights right alongside Xt/yt at line 599-603, then pass rw=rwt into every _select_best(...) call at 619-622, 631-634, 640-651, 659-663, and have _select_best forward it to its internal _evaluate_pipeline call at line 367. This keeps tuning and final-fit weighting consistent while preserving index alignment with the Xt/yt subsample.

all_findings.title: Rows with unparseable dates get MAXIMUM recency weight (1.0), not minimum
all_findings.issue: In _recency_weights, w = np.ones(len(parsed)) and w[i] is only overwritten inside `if p is not None`. So any row whose date fails _parse (returns None) keeps weight 1.0 — the same weight given to the single most-recent match (latest). A match with a bad/missing date is therefore treated as maximally recent and given full influence, while genuinely recent matches with good dates are the only others near 1.0 and all valid older matches are down-weighted. If a batch of rows (e.g. one league/season with a different date format) fails to parse, those rows silently dominate the fit despite possibly being the oldest data.
all_findings.fix: Default failed-parse rows to a low weight rather than 1.0 — e.g. initialize the loop to assign None-parsed rows the minimum computed weight (or treat their age as the maximum observed age: age = (latest - min(valid)).days). At minimum, initialize w with the smallest valid weight instead of np.ones so a parse failure never outranks real recent matches.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A date-format regression in any of the newly added calendar-year leagues (no.1/se.1/... which use different date plumbing) would silently hand those rows top weight, corrupting the recency intent in exactly the code path that was just extended.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:928 initializes `w = np.ones(len(parsed))`, i.e. every row defaults to weight 1.0 (the weight of the single most-recent, `age=0` match). The loop at 929-932 only overwrites `w[i]` when `_parse(d)` succeeded (`p is not None`); rows whose date failed to parse keep the untouched 1.0 default. So a row with a bad/missing date is treated as if it happened on `latest` (maximal recency weight), not down-weighted as stale/unknown data. This exactly matches the finding.
all_findings.corrected_fix: Initialize `w` to the minimum weight actually achievable for the data (i.e. the decay at the maximum observed age) rather than 1.0, so unparseable rows are treated as "as old as it gets" rather than "as new as it gets": e.g. compute `oldest = min(valid)`, `max_age = (latest - oldest).days`, `w = np.full(len(parsed), 0.5 ** (max_age / float(halflife_days)))`, then overwrite in the loop as today. This keeps behavior identical for all valid-date rows and only changes the default for unparseable ones, from 1.0 (max) to the weight of the oldest known match (min) — a safer, non-arbitrary fallback. Equivalent alternative: default to 0.0 (fully ignore rows with unknown dates) if that's preferred over including them at minimum weight.

all_findings.title: SelectKBest uses mutual_info_classif with no random_state -> nondeterministic feature selection
all_findings.issue: SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=select_k) (line 301) is passed the bare mutual_info_classif imported at line 183. mutual_info_classif estimates MI for continuous features with a kNN method that injects random noise; its random_state defaults to None, so it is nondeterministic. This runs both when scoring the k in {50,35,20} candidates during tuning (_select_best -> _evaluate_pipeline) AND in the final pipeline's SelectKBest.fit on the full 167k data. Every other estimator in the file pins random_state=42, but this one does not, so which select_k wins, which features survive, and the persisted feature_importances_ (remapped through get_support() at lines 707-712) all vary run to run. The shipped model.joblib is therefore not reproducible.
all_findings.fix: Pin it: `from functools import partial` and pass `SelectKBest(partial(mutual_info_classif, random_state=42), k=select_k)`. (A functools.partial score_func is accepted by SelectKBest.)
all_findings.why_it_matters: The single most important non-recurring-bug property for a retrainable shipped model is that re-running training reproduces the same artifact; here it silently does not, and feature importances shown in the UI shift between identical runs.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:183 imports mutual_info_classif from sklearn; model_trainer.py:301 does `SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=select_k)` with no random_state pinned. sklearn's mutual_info_classif defaults random_state=None and uses a kNN-based nonparametric MI estimator that adds small random noise to break ties, so its output is nondeterministic between runs. Every other estimator in the file (lines 220-257: RandomForest, HistGradientBoosting, LogisticRegression variants) explicitly pins random_state=42, making this selector the sole unpinned source of randomness. It's exercised both during model-selection tuning (via _select_best -> _evaluate_pipeline scoring select_k in {50,35,20}) and in the final pipeline fit on the full 167k-row dataset, so both the winning k and the selected feature subset can differ across identical reruns, and the feature_importances_ persisted via get_support() remapping would shift accordingly.
all_findings.corrected_fix: Proposed fix is correct and minimal: wrap with functools.partial to pin the seed, e.g. `from functools import partial` then `SelectKBest(partial(mutual_info_classif, random_state=42), k=select_k)`. SelectKBest calls score_func(X, y) so a partial-bound callable works transparently. Apply this everywhere SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, ...) appears (line 301 and any other occurrence found via grep) to ensure both the tuning loop and final refit are deterministic.

all_findings.title: All hyperparameters tuned on the last-8000 date-sorted tail, which in a July retrain is dominated by summer/calendar-year leagues
all_findings.issue: tuning_cap=8000 with Xt,yt = X_arr[-8000:] (lines 599-601) selects select_k, the rf/histgb/lr params, and the voting weights from only the most-recent ~4.8% of 167,495 rows. Rows are globally date-sorted (data_processor.py:48), so the tail is the newest matches. With the 8 newly added calendar-year leagues (MLS/ARG/JPN/CHN/NOR/SWE/FIN/IRL) and a current date of 2026-07-27, that tail is heavily those summer-active competitions while the season-based European leagues the model mostly serves are in their off-season. The winning config (feature count, tree depth, ensemble weights) is thus chosen on a slice that is unrepresentative of the served distribution, and the choice is coupled to whatever leagues happen to be in-season at retrain time.
all_findings.fix: Draw the tuning subsample from across the full dataset instead of the pure recent tail -- e.g. a fixed-seed random (or per-league stratified) sample of ~8000 rows, or raise the cap materially. If a recency bias in tuning is intended, at minimum make it a stratified-by-league sample so no single seasonal cohort dominates candidate selection.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A model whose k, depth and voting weights are picked from Scandinavian/American/Asian summer fixtures but deployed mainly on EPL/LaLiga/etc. can be mistuned in a way that shifts every retrain depending on the calendar.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:599-601 does exactly what the finding describes: tuning_cap=8000, and when len(X_arr) > tuning_cap, Xt, yt = X_arr[-8000:], y_arr[-8000:] — a pure tail slice, no stratification. data_processor.py:48 confirms rows are globally date-sorted (`rows.sort(key=lambda r: r["date"])`) across all leagues combined, not sorted per-league, so the last 8000 rows of the full ~167k-row dataset are whichever matches across ALL leagues happen to be most recent in wall-clock date terms. Given the newly added calendar-year leagues (MLS/ARG1/JPN1/CHN1/NOR1/SWE1/FIN1/IRL1 run roughly Feb/Mar-Nov/Dec) and a July retrain date, while the season-based European leagues (EPL, La Liga, Serie A, etc.) that the model primarily serves are in their summer off-season with no fixtures being generated, the tail-most rows are structurally biased toward the calendar-year cohort at retrain time. This is used to drive select_k, RF/HistGB/LR hyperparameter grids, and (for ensemble/stacking) the base-leg tuning and voting-weight/meta-learner selection at lines 619-660ish — all real model-selection decisions, not just final refit. The finding's mechanism is verified in code exactly as claimed and the seasonal-skew logic is sound, though I did not independently verify the actual per-league date ranges/row counts in the current csv corpus to quantify how dominant the calendar-year leagues are in the tail — that part is inferred from the stated league additions and today's date rather than directly measured.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is reasonable as-is: replace the pure recency-tail slice with a stratified-by-league (or seed-fixed random) sample of ~8000 rows for tuning, e.g. group X/y by league code and take a proportional or capped-per-league sample so no single seasonal cohort dominates the grid search; keep the final refit on the full X_arr unchanged. Alternatively/additionally, log the per-league composition of Xt at tuning time (already have tuning_notes dict) so future audits can directly see whether a given retrain's tuning slice was skewed before trusting the selected config.

all_findings.title: No model.joblib size guard now that Git LFS is removed; grid can produce a >100MB artifact
all_findings.issue: joblib.dump at line 1225 has no size assertion, and main.py performs no size check either. The current artifact is 42.5MB (safe), but the tuning grid can select n_estimators=400 / max_depth up to 12 RF legs wrapped in CalibratedClassifierCV; the in-file comment at lines 233-238 records a past config that produced a 557MB (and 390MB) model.joblib. With Git LFS removed, any artifact over GitHub's 100MB hard limit fails to push, and nothing warns before that happens -- the failure surfaces only at git push, after a multi-hour retrain.
all_findings.fix: After joblib.dump, stat the file and warn/raise when it exceeds a threshold (e.g. >90MB), so an oversized winning config is caught at save time rather than at push. Optionally cap the RF grid's tree-count*depth product for the same reason.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A silent push failure on a non-reproducible retrain (see finding 1) is exactly the kind of late-binding failure the LFS removal traded away the safety net for.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:1222-1227 shows the actual save path: `joblib.dump(self.pipeline, joblib_path)` wrapped in a bare `try/except Exception: pass`, with no size check before or after. No `os.path.getsize`/`os.stat` call on the joblib output exists anywhere in the file or in main.py's train_model_csv. The grid comment at lines 232-238 corroborates this isn't hypothetical: it explicitly records a past n_estimators=500/max_depth=None candidate producing a 557MB (390MB at depth=18) model.joblib, which is exactly why the current RF_GRID (max n_estimators=400, max_depth=12) was chosen. That history note is the only safeguard — it's a comment restraining grid values, not a runtime check — so any future edit to _RF_GRID (or a different model swapped in) that regresses toward a bigger model would silently save/attempt-push with no warning until `git push` fails on GitHub's 100MB limit, post-LFS-removal.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is fine as stated; make it concrete: after each successful joblib.dump call (both pipeline and calibrator), do `size_mb = os.path.getsize(joblib_path) / 1e6` and log a warning if it exceeds ~90MB (leave headroom under GitHub's 100MB hard limit), or raise if it exceeds 100MB outright so a bad retrain fails at save time, not at push time. Since the current code swallows dump exceptions silently (`except Exception: pass`), also add a log line on that except branch — right now a failed dump for any reason (disk, permissions, oversized/corrupt object) is invisible too, not just an oversized one.

all_findings.title: Recency weighting (and its class-weight interaction) is inert in the shipped training path
all_findings.issue: The CLI trains via train_model_csv at main.py:408 without passing recency_halflife_days, so it defaults to None (main.py:108). That flows to model.train(recency_halflife_days=None), _recency_weights returns None (model_trainer.py:913), and the entire recency block -- the sw = sw*rw renormalization in both the CV folds (lines 407-410) and the final refit (lines 682-685) -- never executes for the shipped model. So the newly added recency machinery, and specifically the balanced-class-weight x recency interaction that is a stated concern, is untested in the production path. Separately, that renormalization (sw *= len/sum after multiplying balanced weights by decaying recency) does break the per-class balance when it IS enabled, which is worth validating before wiring it on.
all_findings.fix: Either expose recency_halflife_days through argparse and thread it into the main.py:408 call so the shipped model actually uses (and tests) it, or explicitly document that recency is opt-in and off by default so it is not assumed active. If enabling it, add a test that the combined balanced*recency weights still preserve intended class balance.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A feature that is present, persisted (recency_halflife_days is saved/loaded), and reasoned about in comments but never executed by the only training entrypoint is a maintenance and correctness trap -- reviewers assume the shipped model behaves as the code describes.
all_findings.reason: main.py:408 calls train_model_csv(seasons_arg, train_codes, args.cv_folds, model_type=args.model_type) with no recency_halflife_days argument, so it takes the function's default of None (main.py:108). There is also no argparse option anywhere in main() (lines 266-344) to ever supply a non-None value from the CLI — searched the full arg list, no --recency/--halflife flag exists. That None flows to model.train(recency_halflife_days=None) at main.py:137-138, and model_trainer.py's _recency_weights (line 904, guard at line 913: `if not sample_dates or not halflife_days: return None`) short-circuits to None whenever halflife_days is falsy. So recency_weights is None for train() at line 955, meaning the sw*=rw renormalization blocks in both the CV folds and final refit never execute in the only shipped training entrypoint. recency_halflife_days IS still persisted (model_trainer.py:1213/1277) and documented in train()'s docstring (lines 951-953), matching the "present but inert" characterization exactly.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is accurate and sufficient: add a --recency-halflife-days argparse option in main() and thread it into the train_model_csv call at line 408 (and into train_model_csv's own signature forwarding, which already exists at lines 108/137). No correction needed to the fix itself; additionally worth noting in the fix that since this is currently fully dead code in production, any test added for the balanced-weight x recency interaction should assert on _recency_weights combined with class-balance weights directly (unit level) rather than only via a full CLI run, since CLI-level enabling requires the argparse change first.

all_findings.title: MODEL_VERSION still 3.0.0 after new persisted keys and reworked calibration; load() has no version gate
all_findings.issue: MODEL_VERSION is still "3.0.0" (line 23) despite this changeset adding new persisted fields (calib_C, recency_halflife_days, rps, cv_rps) and reworking calibration/metrics. load() (lines 1242-1330) reads every field with .get and never checks version, so a new-format model.json read by older code silently drops the new keys, and there is no way to tell a new artifact from an old one by version. Combined with the nondeterministic feature selection, two artifacts with identical version strings can differ materially.
all_findings.fix: Bump MODEL_VERSION (e.g. 3.1.0) for the new schema, and optionally warn in load() when the loaded version is older than the running code's MODEL_VERSION.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Version is the only cheap signal that a persisted model matches the code expecting to consume it; leaving it stale defeats its purpose.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py:23 defines MODEL_VERSION = \"3.0.0\" (unchanged), used at line 534 to stamp every newly-trained model. load() (lines 1242-1330) reads version at line 1252 (data.get(\"version\", \"1.0.0\")) purely for display/storage — it is never compared against MODEL_VERSION, and every new field added in this changeset (rps_/cv_rps at 1265-1266, calib_C_/recency_halflife_days at 1276-1277) is pulled with .get() defaults with no version gate or warning. This matches the finding exactly: two artifacts, one pre-changeset and one post-changeset, both self-report \"3.0.0\" despite incompatible schemas, and old code loading a new file (or vice versa) gets silent defaults instead of a signal.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix (bump MODEL_VERSION to e.g. 3.1.0, optionally warn in load() when loaded version < running MODEL_VERSION) is correct and doesn't need correction. Could additionally suggest comparing via a parsed tuple (e.g. packaging.version or a simple tuple split) rather than string compare, since \"3.10.0\" > \"3.9.0\" fails under naive string comparison.

all_findings.title: Duplicate rps / cv_rps keys in the save() metadata dict
all_findings.issue: The metadata dict in save() lists "rps": self.rps_ and "cv_rps": self.cv_rps twice -- once at lines 1200-1201 and again at lines 1214-1215. Python keeps only the last occurrence, so it is harmless, but it is dead duplicate literal keys that signal a copy-paste slip and can mislead a future editor into thinking one copy differs.
all_findings.fix: Delete the duplicate "rps"/"cv_rps" entries at lines 1214-1215.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Minor, but duplicate dict-literal keys are a code smell that lint/CI often flags and that obscures intent in the save schema.
all_findings.reason: model_trainer.py's save() metadata dict literal contains "rps": self.rps_ and "cv_rps": self.cv_rps at lines 1200-1201, then repeats the identical keys "rps": self.rps_ / "cv_rps": self.cv_rps again at lines 1214-1215 (verified by direct read of lines 1185-1220). Since it's a Python dict literal, the second occurrence simply overwrites the first with the same value — functionally harmless (json.dump output is unaffected), but it is a duplicate-key copy-paste artifact.
all_findings.corrected_fix: Delete lines 1214-1215 (the second "rps"/"cv_rps" entries), keeping the originals at lines 1200-1201.

all_findings.title: Squad-value coverage forfeited for 5 of 8 new leagues that Transfermarkt actually covers
all_findings.issue: The 8 new leagues have no LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP entry, so build_club_mapping() hits `comp = LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP.get(...)` -> None -> `continue` (club_mapping.py:165-166) and every club gets has_squad_value=0. This is described as 'unavoidable — Transfermarkt doesn't cover them', but that is false for most of them. Inspecting the cached data_cache/transfermarkt_clubs.csv shows the dataset DOES carry these exact domestic competitions: NO1 (Norway, 19 clubs), SE1 (Sweden, 19), JAP1 (Japan, 23), MLS1 (USA, 30), ARG1 (Argentina, 32) — ~123 clubs whose squad value is being discarded for lack of a one-line mapping each. Only fi.1/FIN1, ie.1/IRL1, cn.1/CHN1 are genuinely absent from clubs.csv. This is the single largest driver of the coverage collapse to ~34% (team_stats.json: only 425/1112 teams carry a value), and most of it is recoverable.
all_findings.fix: Add to LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP: "NOR1": "NO1", "SWE1": "SE1", "JPN1": "JAP1", "MLS": "MLS1", "ARG1": "ARG1". Then run the mapping and inspect which of those clubs resolve via the exact/containment/0.90 tiers vs. fall through; add MANUAL_CLUB_MAP entries (and KNOWN_ABSENT where appropriate) for the non-confident names exactly as was done for the existing leagues, so no wrong join slips in. Leave FIN1/IRL1/CHN1 unmapped (correctly has_squad_value=0).
all_findings.why_it_matters: The module docstring says squad value exists precisely to give cross-league strength comparison a causal signal. Leaving MLS/Argentina/Scandinavia/Japan unmapped when their data is sitting in the already-downloaded clubs.csv throws away the strongest team-strength feature for exactly the newly added leagues and for every cross-league tie involving them.
all_findings.reason: club_mapping.py:39-44 LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP has no keys for NOR1/SWE1/FIN1/IRL1/MLS/JPN1/CHN1/ARG1, so build_club_mapping's `comp = LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP.get(info.get("league",""))` returns None and the loop `continue`s at line 166-167, leaving every team in these 8 leagues with squad_value_eur=None (verified in team_stats.json: 0/30 NOR1, 0/36 SWE1, 0/23 FIN1, 0/22 IRL1, 0/31 MLS, 0/32 JPN1, 0/45 CHN1, 0/45 ARG1 have a value; overall only 425/1112 teams do, matching the ~34% cited). Directly inspected data_cache/transfermarkt_clubs.csv's domestic_competition_id column: NO1=19 clubs, SE1=19, MLS1=30, JAP1=23, ARG1=32 rows present — real, non-empty data for exactly the 5 leagues the finding names as recoverable. FI1, IE1, and CN1 (and JPN1/CN1/AR1 variant codes) each returned 0 rows, confirming those three are genuinely absent as the finding also states. The claim is precisely accurate on both the missing-mapping mechanism and the underlying data availability.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is correct: add "NOR1": "NO1", "SWE1": "SE1", "MLS": "MLS1", "JPN1": "JAP1", "ARG1": "ARG1" to LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP (note ARG1 is both our code and the TM comp id here, unlike the others). After adding, re-run build_club_mapping and manually inspect the auto-resolved (exact/containment/0.90-similarity) matches per the file's own tiering discipline, then hand-add MANUAL_CLUB_MAP/KNOWN_ABSENT entries for anything that falls through unmatched — do not add entries from similarity score alone, consistent with the module's stated policy. Leave FIN1/IRL1/CHN1 out of LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP since their Transfermarkt competition rows are confirmed empty (0 rows for FI1/IE1/CN1 in transfermarkt_clubs.csv).

all_findings.title: The recurring-bug guard test never exercises the squad-value serving path
all_findings.issue: Squad value is populated on TWO different code paths from TWO different source tables: training uses value_at() over player_valuations (data_processor.py:173-174), serving uses current_value() over players.csv baked into team_stats.json (data_processor.py:903-907). This is exactly the train/serve divergence shape the HANDOFF says has bitten five times. Yet TestLiveFeaturesMatchTrainingDistribution (the guard test) only covers season_progress and the venue-split block — it never builds a SquadValueIndex or a club_map. The squad tests in TestSquadValueFeatures (lines 407-460) only exercise the shared arithmetic helper squad_value_feature_dict() and the squad_values=None fallback. Nothing asserts that a MAPPED matchup driven through compute_team_stats()+prepare_prediction_features() yields has_squad_value==1 with a populated home_squad_value. So if players.csv were empty/stale at train time (load_table falls back to a stale per-file cache independently of player_valuations, transfermarkt_data.py:78-86), every current_value would be None, has_squad_value would silently be 0 for ALL live predictions while the model was trained on real value_at values, and no test would fail.
all_findings.fix: Add a test that builds a SquadValueIndex from a few fixture player_valuations + players rows, builds a club_map for two fixture teams, runs add_form_features(..., squad_values, club_map) and compute_team_stats(..., squad_values, club_map), then asserts prepare_prediction_features(...) returns has_squad_value==1.0 and home_squad_value>0 for the mapped pair (and 0 for an unmapped pair). This closes the same class the venue-split tests close.
all_findings.why_it_matters: This is the documented single most important audit question. The feature is currently alive (team_stats.json has 425 real values), but nothing guards it, so the sixth instance of the recurring bug would ship undetected.
all_findings.reason: Reading tests/test_data_processor.py:407-460 (TestSquadValueFeatures) confirms it only calls the pure arithmetic helper squad_value_feature_dict(h, a) directly with hand-picked numbers, or exercises add_form_features(rows, squad_values=None, club_map=None) for the graceful-fallback case (line 456-460). Reading TestLiveFeaturesMatchTrainingDistribution (lines 578-654+) confirms its _built() fixture (line 589-597) never passes squad_values/club_map into add_form_features, and its test methods cover only season_progress and the venue-split form/goals/matches_played/gd_5 block — none constructs a SquadValueIndex or club_map or calls compute_team_stats(..., squad_values, club_map) / prepare_prediction_features to check has_squad_value/home_squad_value on a live path. This matches the finding's description of the actual divergence: data_processor.py:173-174 (training) calls squad_values.value_at(club_map.get(home,''), match_date) against player_valuations-backed data, while data_processor.py:907 (serving, inside compute_team_stats) calls squad_values.current_value(club_id) — a different method/table read at prediction time. No test in the file exercises current_value() through the compute_team_stats->prepare_prediction_features chain with a populated SquadValueIndex, so a divergence between value_at and current_value (e.g. current_value silently returning None due to a stale/empty players.csv cache) would produce has_squad_value==0 for all live predictions while training saw real values, and no test would catch it — exactly the fifth-time-repeated bug class the HANDOFF describes.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is directionally correct and doesn't need major correction. Concretely: add a test class (e.g. TestSquadValueServingPath) that (1) builds a small transfermarkt_data.SquadValueIndex from fixture player_valuations + players rows for two clubs with distinct known values, (2) builds a club_map mapping two fixture team names to those club ids, (3) runs rows = add_form_features(fixture_rows, squad_values=index, club_map=club_map) and stats = compute_team_stats(rows, squad_values=index, club_map=club_map), (4) calls prepare_prediction_features(team_a, team_b, stats, ...) and asserts has_squad_value==1.0 and home_squad_value>0 for the mapped pair, and has_squad_value==0.0 for a team not present in club_map. Additionally assert that the value compute_team_stats derives via current_value(club_id) for a given as-of date is consistent with (not silently zero relative to) what value_at() would have produced in add_form_features for the same club/date, so a future swap of the serving-side lookup method for the training-side one is caught by this guard test the same way the other four regressions are.

all_findings.title: both-sides has_squad_value rule silently voids squad value for cross-league matchups against uncovered leagues
all_findings.issue: squad_value_feature_dict sets `both = bool(home_value) and bool(away_value)` and zeroes the entire block (including squad_value_diff) unless BOTH clubs are known. Post-expansion, one side of an arbitrary cross-league tie is very often in an uncovered/unmapped league, so has_squad_value=0 and squad value contributes nothing — for precisely the cross-league comparisons the feature was built to inform. The both-sides rule is itself defensible (a one-sided value would read the missing side as an infinitely weak squad), but combined with the expanded, unmapped league set it multiplies the ~34% coverage into a much smaller effective match-level coverage.
all_findings.fix: Primary mitigation is finding #1 (map the 5 recoverable leagues). Separately, evaluate whether keeping has_squad_value=0 but still passing a bounded one-sided signal, or adding a distinct 'one_side_known' indicator, beats hard-zeroing both — but only if an ablation on odds_benchmark/CV shows it helps; otherwise leave the conservative rule and rely on #1.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Without addressing coverage, every Man City vs (Argentine/MLS/Scandinavian club) prediction — the headline cross-league use case — gets zero squad signal even though City's value is known.
all_findings.reason: data_processor.py:127 `both = bool(home_value) and bool(away_value)` does gate the whole block as described — lines 130-134 zero home_squad_value/away_squad_value/squad_value_diff/abs_squad_value_diff and has_squad_value unless BOTH sides resolve to a truthy value. `_squad_value_features` (lines 169-175) feeds this from `club_map.get(home, "")`/`club_map.get(away, "")`, so any team missing from Transfermarkt's club_map (plausible for the newly added NOR1/SWE1/FIN1/IRL1/MLS/JPN1/CHN1/ARG1 leagues) forces both=False and zeros the diff even when the other side's value is well known. This is the same shared helper used by both add_form_features (training) and prepare_prediction_features (serving) per the docstring (lines 119-121), so it is a coverage/effectiveness gap rather than a train/serve mismatch — the model does learn has_squad_value=0 as a real recurring state rather than being surprised by it at serving time. The finding's severity (medium, correctness) and description are accurate; the "both-sides rule is defensible but multiplies coverage down" framing is exactly what the code does.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is reasonable as stated (map more leagues first per finding #1; only consider a one-sided signal/indicator if an ablation shows it helps). One addition: since this rule is symmetric across train/serve (not a train/serve mismatch), any change should be validated via odds_benchmark.py RPS/CV rather than treated as a correctness bug fix — the current behavior is intentional and self-consistent, just low-coverage for the expanded cross-league league set.

all_findings.title: train_model() (API path) omits squad args and overwrites team_stats.json with all-None squad values
all_findings.issue: The non-CSV training path calls add_form_features(rows) (main.py:80) and compute_team_stats(rows) (main.py:101) with no squad_values/club_map, then save_artifacts() (main.py:102) writes team_stats.json with squad_value_eur=None for every team. If this path is ever run after the shipped CSV-trained model (train_model_csv, which DOES enrich squad values — csv_data_loader.py:655-676), it silently clobbers team_stats.json so the shipped model — trained with real squad features — serves has_squad_value=0 for every prediction. Classic silent train/serve divergence introduced by an artifact overwrite.
all_findings.fix: Either build squad_values/club_map in train_model() the same way csv_data_loader does and pass them to both add_form_features and compute_team_stats, or have this path refuse to overwrite an existing squad-enriched team_stats.json. At minimum log the mapped/covered count as csv_data_loader.py:658-660 does, so a zero-coverage artifact write is visible.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Two training entry points writing the same artifact with incompatible feature coverage is exactly how a populated-in-training / degenerate-in-serving feature ships.
all_findings.reason: main.py:101 calls compute_team_stats(rows) with no squad_values/club_map args. compute_team_stats's signature (data_processor.py:768) defaults both to None, and its per-team default (data_processor.py:784) sets squad_value_eur=None; the only place that sets a real value is data_processor.py:907 (info["squad_value_eur"] = squad_values.current_value(club_id)), which is only reached when squad_values is provided. main.py:102 then calls save_artifacts(metrics, api_team_stats), which writes this all-null-squad dict straight to team_stats.json (verified by save_artifacts signature at main.py:150). The current team_stats.json in the repo has real non-null squad_value_eur figures for large clubs (e.g. lines 9202/9312/10467 in the millions), proving it was produced by the CSV path (csv_data_loader.py enriches squad values before calling compute_team_stats in train_model_csv). If train_model_api is ever invoked after that, it silently overwrites the enriched file with a version where every team has squad_value_eur=None, producing exactly the train/serve divergence pattern this codebase has repeatedly suffered from.
all_findings.corrected_fix: Proposed fix is sound as written: either (a) have train_model_api build squad_values/club_map the same way csv_data_loader.py does (lines ~655-676) and pass them into both add_form_features and compute_team_stats, or (b) make save_artifacts/train_model_api refuse to overwrite an existing team_stats.json's squad_value_eur values with an all-null set (e.g., detect that api_team_stats has zero non-null squad values while the existing file has some, and warn/abort instead of silently overwriting). Also log the enrichment coverage count in train_model_api the way csv_data_loader.py:658-660 does, so a zero-coverage write is visible in the console output rather than silent.

all_findings.title: value_at (training) can overstate current roster relative to current_value (serving)
all_findings.issue: build() derives point-in-time totals from player_state, which retains a player at his last-valued club until a NEW valuation reassigns him (transfermarkt_data.py:156-161). A departed player therefore keeps inflating his old club's value_at total for months, while current_value (players.csv current_club_id, lines 180-195) reflects the actual current roster. Measured over the 1026 clubs present in both, cur/value_at has median 1.0 but p10=0.68 — a meaningful left tail where the training-time value is materially higher than the serving-time value for the same club. The model learns weights on the (sometimes inflated) value_at scale and applies them to the current_value scale at serve time.
all_findings.fix: Low priority given median 1.0. If tightened, either (a) decay/expire player_state entries not re-valued within N months so departed players stop counting, or (b) source current from the latest value_at snapshot instead of players.csv (trading off new-signing responsiveness). Only worth doing if a CV/odds_benchmark check shows the tail hurts.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A systematic train/serve scale offset on the strongest strength feature can bias live probabilities for the affected clubs even when the feature is 'present' on both sides.
all_findings.reason: transfermarkt_data.py:154-172 shows player_state[pid] is only overwritten when a NEW valuation row for that player is processed (line 157: player_state[pid] = (val, cid)); the totals used for value_at() snapshots (lines 160-172) sum whatever club each player's most recent valuation says, so a player transferred without a fresh valuation keeps being counted toward his old club indefinitely in training data. current_value() (line 213-214) instead reads self.current, built at lines 180-195 directly from players.csv current_club_id, which reflects the actual present roster regardless of valuation recency. This is a real, verifiable asymmetry: value_at (used in training via data_processor.py:173-174 _squad_value_features) and current_value (used in serving via data_processor.py:907 compute_team_stats) are computed by genuinely different logic paths that can diverge for the same club. The finding's severity framing (low, median 1.0 with a left tail) and category (consistency, not the hard degenerate-feature bug class) both match what the code shows — it's a soft distributional/scale drift, not a broken feature.
all_findings.corrected_fix: Fix as proposed is reasonable; the code detail worth adding is that the divergence specifically requires a transfer with no fresh valuation event — the freeze-per-month snapshot logic (lines 160-172) is otherwise correct and already avoids double counting once a new valuation lands. Option (a) (expire player_state entries not revalued within N months, e.g. treat them as vacated the roster rather than assuming they stayed) is the more targeted fix since it directly closes the "stale club assignment" gap without changing how current-day serving values are sourced.

all_findings.title: New-league feeds split one club across two team_stats keys (spelling variants)
all_findings.issue: The new-leagues feed uses inconsistent raw team names for the SAME club, and parse_fd_couk_new_csv ingests them verbatim (home_team/away_team, csv_data_loader.py:357-358). compute_team_stats keys purely by that raw string (data_processor.py:848-849 -> team_stats[row['home_team']]), and there is no training-name canonicalization anywhere (team_aliases.py only bridges live-API -> training, not within training). I confirmed in the SHIPPED team_stats.json that all of these coexist as separate keys, each holding only part of the club's real match history: 'Ham-Kam' AND 'HamKam' (NOR1; 50 vs 83 raw appearances), 'Colon Santa FE' AND 'Colon Santa Fe' (ARG1; 420 vs 66), 'Oster' AND 'Osters' (SWE1; Osters IF, 32 vs 30 -- distinct from the separate club 'Ostersunds'). Each club's Elo / Dixon-Coles / rolling-form ratings are therefore computed over a fragmented subset of its games, and h2h/opponent histories reference two different keys for the same team. Same failure family as the recurring bug (a team's real signal is only partly present), just caused by name duplication rather than a train/serve gap.
all_findings.fix: Canonicalize training-data team names before keying. Add a small verified training-name alias/normalization map (e.g. {'HamKam':'Ham-Kam','Colon Santa FE':'Colon Santa Fe','Osters':'Oster'} plus any others found by scanning each new league for names that normalize identically) and apply it to home/away in parse_fd_couk_new_csv (and parse_csv_matches) so variant spellings collapse to one key. Do NOT use fuzzy matching -- only hand-verified exact-string variants, consistent with the project's no-fuzzy constraint.
all_findings.why_it_matters: These clubs now exist in the model but predict off half their history and a stale/duplicated rating, silently returning confident-but-degraded numbers -- exactly the class of bug HANDOFF.md warns about.
all_findings.reason: Verified directly. csv_data_loader.py:357-358 (parse_fd_couk_new_csv) takes `row.get('Home')`/`row.get('Away')` verbatim with only `.strip()` — no normalization, alias map, or lookup table applied (confirmed no 'alias' references anywhere in csv_data_loader.py). data_processor.py:848-849 in compute_team_stats then keys the defaultdict purely by that raw string (`home = row["home_team"]`; `team_stats[home][...]`), with identical raw-string keying used throughout add_form_features for training. The shipped team_stats.json contains all three claimed duplicate-club pairs as distinct top-level keys: 'HamKam' (line 2697) and 'Ham-Kam' (line 43617), 'Colon Santa Fe' (line 43232) and 'Colon Santa FE' (line 46202), 'Oster' (line 37677) and 'Osters' (line 60282) — separate from the genuinely distinct club 'Ostersunds' (line 47852). Since team_stats/Elo/Dixon-Coles ratings and rolling form are accumulated by iterating rows keyed on these raw strings, each spelling variant accumulates only the subset of matches recorded under that exact spelling, fragmenting the club's true history exactly as described. This matches the project's own recurring-bug pattern (a team's real signal only partially present) even though the mechanism here is name duplication within the training feed rather than a train/serve split.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is directionally correct and consistent with the no-fuzzy-matching constraint: add a small hand-verified normalization dict (e.g. {'HamKam': 'Ham-Kam', 'Colon Santa FE': 'Colon Santa Fe', 'Osters': 'Oster'}) applied to home_team/away_team immediately after strip() in parse_fd_couk_new_csv (and audit parse_csv_matches / other new-league parsers for the same issue, plus scan all 8 new leagues' raw CSVs for other exact-duplicate spellings, not just the 3 sampled here). One refinement: apply the same normalization at the team_aliases.py live-API bridge too if any of these clubs are reachable from the live UI, so a live lookup doesn't hit the pre-canonicalization key.

all_findings.title: team_aliases has zero new-league clubs, so their data is unreachable from the offered CL/EC fixtures
all_findings.issue: The 8 new leagues are training-only and correctly absent from config.LEAGUE_CODES, but that dropdown DOES offer CL, EC and WC (config.py:33-35). New-league clubs (e.g. Bodo/Glimt, Molde, Rosenborg from NOR1; Malmo FF from SWE1) regularly appear in those competitions and are now present in team_stats. TEAM_NAME_ALIASES (team_aliases.py:31-114) contains no entry for any of them, and their training keys (e.g. 'Bodo/Glimt', 'Malmo FF') will not exact-match football-data.org's official CL names (e.g. 'FK Bodo/Glimt', 'Malmo FF'). resolve_team_name will fail closed and the fixture falls back to a neutral prediction even though real stats exist. The module's own 'verified leagues' note (lines 28-30) also still omits CL despite CL alias entries already living in the table (lines 86-89), so the table's scope is understated.
all_findings.fix: Add hand-verified aliases (against team_stats.json) for the new-league clubs that actually reach CL/EC/WC, or, if that is out of scope, add a one-line comment in team_aliases.py stating new-league clubs are intentionally unreachable from Fixtures so a future maintainer does not read it as an oversight. Update the 'verified leagues' note on line 28-30 to include CL.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Without it, the just-added Scandinavian/other data can never influence a live prediction, so the coverage work is partly wasted for the one path (European cups) where those clubs are actually offerable.
all_findings.reason: All claims verified directly in code: (1) config.py:33-35 confirms CL/EC/WC are in LEAGUE_CODES, and app.py:233-277 passes this exact dict as `leagues=LEAGUE_CODES` to fixtures.html, so they are genuinely offered on the Fixtures dropdown. (2) team_stats.json contains real entries for the new-league clubs the finding names: "Bodo/Glimt" (line 2642), "Malmo FF" (3357), "Molde" (4787), "Rosenborg" (4952) — confirming training data exists for them. (3) team_aliases.py:31-114 (TEAM_NAME_ALIASES) has zero entries for any of these strings (grep for bodo|molde|rosenborg|malmo|glimt case-insensitively returns nothing). (4) resolve_team_name (team_aliases.py:117-129) does an exact match against team_stats first, then a normalized lookup only through TEAM_NAME_ALIASES, returning None if neither hits — a football-data.org CL name like "FK Bodø/Glimt" normalizes to "fk bodo/glimt", which is not a key in team_stats nor in TEAM_NAME_ALIASES, so resolution fails. (5) app.py:172-173 confirms the failure mode: `home_lookup = home_team if home_team in stats else (resolve_team_name(home_team, stats) or home_team)` — on failure it falls back to the raw unresolved API name, which is absent from stats, so the club is effectively treated as unknown/neutral even though its real stats exist. (6) The comment at team_aliases.py:28-30 says aliases were "verified... for PL, PD, BL1, SA, FL1, DED, PPL, ELC — the leagues actually offered on the Fixtures page," but CL alias entries already exist at lines 86-89 (Benfica, Sp Lisbon, St. Gilloise, FC Copenhagen) and CL is demonstrably offered per app.py — so the note's own scope statement is inconsistent with the code beneath it, exactly as the finding states. Severity "low" is appropriate: this is a silent coverage gap (fails closed to an honest neutral/unknown fallback) rather than a corruption or wrong-prediction bug, consistent with the module's stated exact-or-nothing design philosophy.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is directionally right; tightening it: add verified aliases only for clubs confirmed to actually reach CL/EC (e.g. "Bodo/Glimt", "Malmo FF", "Molde", "Rosenborg" — confirmed present in team_stats.json at the exact keys used above) once their live football-data.org CL/EC roster names are checked by hand (do not guess the accented/prefixed form, e.g. "FK Bodø/Glimt" vs "Bodø / Glimt"). At minimum, update the comment at team_aliases.py:28-30 to add "CL" to the verified-leagues list (since CL entries already exist at lines 86-89) and either add the new-league aliases or add an explicit one-line comment noting new-league (NOR1/SWE1/etc.) clubs are currently unreachable from Fixtures by design, so it isn't mistaken for an oversight later.

all_findings.title: New leagues undocumented in LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP; squad values silently forgone
all_findings.issue: LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP (club_mapping.py:39-44) still lists only the pre-existing leagues; the 8 new standard codes (NOR1/SWE1/FIN1/IRL1/MLS/JPN1/CHN1/ARG1) are absent. The behaviour is SAFE -- build_club_mapping does comp=LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP.get(...) and `if not comp: continue` (lines 165-166), so new-league teams simply get no squad value (has_squad_value=0), consistently in both training and serving, so this is NOT the recurring train/serve bug. But the accompanying comment only excuses lower divisions ('eng.2-5, es.2 ... intentionally absent'); it does not mention the new top-flight leagues, several of which Transfermarkt does cover (MLS, Argentina, J-League), so a maintainer cannot tell whether the omission was deliberate or an oversight. NOTE (verification, not a defect): I checked the cached data and found NO exact or normalized cross-league name collision between any of the 8 new leagues and the existing mapped leagues -- Argentine clubs are named distinctly ('Arsenal Sarandi', 'Racing Club', 'Independiente'), so the new leagues create no wrong Transfermarkt join.
all_findings.fix: Extend the comment in LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP to enumerate the 8 new leagues as intentionally unmapped (mirroring the lower-division note), or add the mappings for the ones Transfermarkt covers to gain squad-value signal for MLS/Argentina/Japan.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Cheap clarity fix that prevents the omission from being mistaken later for the very train/serve degeneracy this codebase keeps re-introducing.
all_findings.reason: club_mapping.py:39-44 LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP contains only the 19 pre-existing league codes (PL, PD, BL1, SA, FL1, DED, PPL, BEL1, TUR1, GRE1, RUS1, POL1, AUT1, SUI1, DEN1, ROU1, BSA, SCO1, MEX1); none of the 8 new codes from csv_data_loader.py (NOR1, SWE1, FIN1, IRL1, MLS, JPN1, CHN1, ARG1, confirmed present at csv_data_loader.py:172-179) appear. build_club_mapping (lines 164-167) does `comp = LEAGUE_TO_TM_COMP.get(info.get('league', ''), ...); if not comp: continue`, so teams in these 8 leagues are simply skipped -> no squad_value mapping, consistently at both train and serve time (has_squad_value=0 both places) -- this is safe, not the train/serve degeneracy bug the audit is hunting for. The explanatory comment at lines 36-38 only justifies omitting lower divisions ('eng.2-5, es.2, de.2, it.2, fr.2, sco.2-4') and says nothing about the 8 new top-flight leagues, several of which (MLS, Argentina Primera, J1 League) Transfermarkt does cover, so a maintainer can't tell intentional-exclusion from oversight. Severity is correctly low/documentation-only.
all_findings.corrected_fix: No correction needed; the proposed fix (extend the comment to enumerate the 8 new leagues as intentionally unmapped, and optionally add TM domestic_competition_id mappings for MLS/ARG1/JPN1 if squad-value signal is wanted) is accurate as written.

all_findings.title: Flask runs with debug=True bound to 0.0.0.0 (network-exposed interactive debugger / RCE)
all_findings.issue: app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True) exposes the Werkzeug interactive debugger on every network interface. Any unhandled exception in a route (and there is at least one unguarded exception path — see the /predict finding) opens the traceback console, whose PIN-protected eval shell allows arbitrary Python execution. Combined with 0.0.0.0 this is reachable from any host on the LAN, not just localhost. debug=True also enables the auto-reloader, inappropriate for a shipped/demo artifact.
all_findings.fix: Set debug=False (or gate it: debug=os.environ.get('FLASK_DEBUG')=='1') and bind host="127.0.0.1" unless external access is explicitly needed. e.g. app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=5000, debug=False).
all_findings.why_it_matters: A single route exception on a machine reachable by others becomes remote code execution.
all_findings.reason: app.py:302 reads exactly `app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True)` inside `if __name__ == "__main__":` (lines 300-302), with no environment-variable gate or config check. This binds to all network interfaces with Werkzeug's interactive debugger enabled. Any unhandled exception in any route (train() at line 295-297 does catch broadly, but that's only one route — other routes/handlers may not) would expose the Werkzeug debugger console, whose PIN-based console still permits arbitrary code execution once triggered, and it's reachable from any host that can reach port 5000, not just localhost.
all_findings.corrected_fix: Bind to 127.0.0.1 and disable debug for any non-local run, e.g.: `app.run(host=os.environ.get("HOST", "127.0.0.1"), port=5000, debug=os.environ.get("FLASK_DEBUG") == "1")`. If LAN access is genuinely required for demo purposes, keep debug=False and rely on the app's own error handling/logging instead of the interactive debugger.

all_findings.title: POST /train is destructive — clobbers the shipped 167k-match ensemble with a 5-league logreg
all_findings.issue: train() calls train_model_csv(seasons=["2021-22","2022-23","2023-24"], top5=["eng.1","es.1","de.1","it.1","fr.1"], cv_folds=3, model_type="logreg"). train_model_csv (main.py:107-147) then overwrites model.json/model.joblib via model.save(), and team_stats.json + processed_data.json + h2h_stats.json via save_processed_data/save_artifacts — using data from only 5 leagues / 3 seasons. This replaces the shipped 1112-team / 32-league / 85-feature ensemble with a logreg whose team_stats cover only the top-5 leagues, so build_team_stats() (which prefers team_stats.json) would afterwards feed the Predict chooser just 5 leagues, and the dashboard tag (metrics.model_type) would read 'logreg' while the copy still says 'ensemble'. There is no confirmation, no backup, and the route is always live even though the 'Train model now' button is normally hidden (model_exists() is True).
all_findings.fix: Remove the /train route and the two 'Train model now' buttons (predict.html:78-80 and the no-model card), since the app ships a pre-trained model. If a retrain trigger must stay, make it non-destructive (write to a temp path / require an explicit confirm token) and use the full league+season set with model_type="ensemble" so it cannot silently downgrade the production artifacts.
all_findings.why_it_matters: One POST permanently degrades the deployed model and roster with no undo.
all_findings.reason: app.py:282-297 defines POST /train, unconditionally calling train_model_csv(seasons=[\"2021-22\",\"2022-23\",\"2023-24\"], top5=[\"eng.1\",\"es.1\",\"de.1\",\"it.1\",\"fr.1\"], cv_folds=3, model_type=\"logreg\") with no auth/confirmation. main.py:107-147 shows train_model_csv calls model.save() (model_trainer.py:1185-1187, defaults to model.json/model.joblib in _SCRIPT_DIR — the same path the shipped model uses), then save_processed_data(...) and save_artifacts(metrics, team_stats, h2h_map=h2h_map), which write processed_data.json/team_stats.json/h2h_stats.json. All of this uses only 5 leagues x 3 seasons, so it overwrites the 167k-match/32-league/85-feature production artifacts with a small logreg's outputs, no backup, no undo. The route's only gating is that the 'Train model now' button is hidden in the UI when model_exists() is True (predict.html:74, app.py:86/188/198) — the POST endpoint itself is still live and reachable regardless (e.g., via curl), so the finding's core claim (destructive overwrite, no confirmation, endpoint always live) is accurate as stated.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The original fix is reasonable; refine slightly: since the button is UI-gated (not fully unconditional at the frontend), the real gap is that the backend route has no server-side protection. Either (a) remove /train entirely since a pretrained model.joblib ships with the repo, or (b) if a retrain path must remain, guard it server-side (e.g., require an explicit confirmation token/header, write to a temp path and require a second explicit 'promote' step, or check model_exists() server-side and 403 if a model is already deployed) and use the full league/season set with model_type=\"ensemble\" instead of a 5-league logreg, so a stray POST cannot silently downgrade the production model/team_stats/h2h artifacts.

all_findings.title: /predict has no error handling around feature-build and model.predict (stale-artifact mismatch → unhandled 500)
all_findings.issue: Lines 201-202 call prepare_prediction_features(...) and model.predict(features) with no try/except, and predict() never checks len(features) against model.feature_names. If model.json/model.joblib were trained with a different feature count/order than the current data_processor produces (exactly the stale-artifact mismatch this audit is worried about), sklearn's pipeline.predict_proba (model_trainer.py:1047) raises ValueError. Unlike the /fixtures route (which wraps API calls) and every other user-facing path, this bubbles up as a raw 500 / debug traceback. A malformed stats row for a resolved team would do the same.
all_findings.fix: Wrap the prediction block in try/except and re-render predict.html with an error. Optionally add an explicit guard before predict: if model.feature_names and len(features) != len(model.feature_names): render an 'model/data version mismatch' error instead of predicting. Mirror the pattern already used in /fixtures.
all_findings.why_it_matters: The exact recurring failure mode of this codebase (train/serve feature drift) would surface as an ugly crash rather than a handled message, and with debug=True as an RCE console.
all_findings.reason: app.py:201-202 calls prepare_prediction_features(...) and model.predict(features) with zero exception handling, unlike /fixtures (app.py:242-244, wraps API/lookup errors) and /train (app.py:292-295, wraps TrainingError/MissingTokenError/Exception). There is no feature-count/order guard anywhere in app.py (grep for 'feature_names' in app.py returns nothing outside model_trainer.py internals). app.run at line 302 has debug=True, so an unhandled exception here would render Werkzeug's interactive debugger. This is exactly the failure mode the audit is worried about: if model.joblib's expected feature vector (built at fit time) diverges from what prepare_prediction_features currently emits, sklearn's pipeline will raise (typically ValueError for shape mismatch, or a scaler/column mismatch error) and it will propagate straight out of the route.

all_findings.title: model_exists() and get_model() disagree when model.joblib is missing/corrupt
all_findings.issue: model_exists() returns True whenever model.json is present, but MatchPredictorModel.load() (model_trainer.py:1294-1308) only returns True if the .joblib pipeline (or legacy NB state) actually loads. The 42MB model.joblib is precisely the file at risk of not reaching GitHub now that Git LFS was removed. If model.json ships but model.joblib does not, model_exists() reports True: the dashboard boasts full metrics and the Predict page renders the chooser, yet every prediction quietly falls back to the 'No trained model' card (predict route lines 197-199). The user sees a healthy app that never predicts.
all_findings.fix: Make model_exists() reflect what get_model() can actually load, e.g. check that both model.json and model.joblib exist (os.path.exists('model.joblib')), or implement model_exists as `get_model() is not None`. Keep the dashboard's 'no model' copy consistent with that.
all_findings.why_it_matters: A partial artifact deploy produces a silently non-functional predictor that still advertises full metrics.
all_findings.reason: app.py:87 model_exists() checks only os.path.exists(model.json). model_trainer.py load() (1242-1330) requires either a loadable pipeline from model.joblib (self.pipeline is not None at line 1300, returns True at 1308) or legacy means/priors keys in model.json (1311-1328); otherwise returns False at line 1330. Current training path (main.py) saves an sklearn pipeline, not legacy means/priors, so if model.joblib is missing or fails joblib.load (caught silently at 1296-1298, leaving self.pipeline None), load() falls through to the legacy check, finds no means/priors, and returns False -> get_model() returns None -> app.py:90-92. Meanwhile model_exists() still returns True since model.json alone is present. This is exactly the scenario flagged: a partial deploy (missing/corrupt 42MB model.joblib) makes the app advertise a working model while every prediction silently fails.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The suggested fix is reasonable; simplest robust version: replace model_exists() with `return get_model() is not None` (or cache the loaded model) so the check always mirrors what get_model() can actually load, rather than duplicating the joblib-existence check (which would miss the joblib.load() exception case at model_trainer.py:1294-1298).

all_findings.title: evaluation.per_league is written to evaluation.json but no longer rendered by the app
all_findings.issue: per_league_breakdown is still computed and stored under evaluation.json['per_league'] (evaluate.py:295) and printed by the CLI (308-310), but the dashboard's per-league card was removed, so dashboard.html no longer reads the field (confirmed: no 'per_league' reference in templates/). league_options() and LEAGUE_NAMES remain in active use (the Predict league picker), so only the per_league JSON payload is now dead as far as the web UI is concerned — not the whole breakdown, which the CLI still prints.
all_findings.fix: Leave the CLI print, but consider dropping the per_league key from the persisted evaluation.json (or re-adding a per-league section to dashboard.html if the data is still wanted in the UI) so the shipped JSON doesn't carry a payload nothing renders.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Minor: harmless stale data in the committed artifact; only worth a cleanup, not a fix.
all_findings.reason: evaluate.py:295 computes per_league_breakdown(...) and stores it under out["per_league"], which is JSON-dumped into evaluation.json at line 299-300, and printed by the CLI at lines 307-310. A repo-wide grep for "per_league" finds it only in evaluate.py and the two evaluation*.json artifacts — zero matches in templates/ (dashboard.html, predict.html, or any other template). This matches the claim in the finding: the per-league card was removed from the UI per the task's own changelog note, so the per_league payload written to evaluation.json is no longer consumed by anything in the web app, even though the CLI still computes and prints it. league_options()/LEAGUE_NAMES are a separate, still-used code path (Predict picker), so the finding's scoping is accurate too.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is reasonable as stated (drop the per_league key from the persisted JSON, or re-add a per-league UI section) — no correction needed. One addition: since the CLI print block (evaluate.py:307-310) reads from out["per_league"], if the key is dropped from the dict before json.dump, the print loop must be pointed at a local variable instead (e.g. keep per_league_breakdown(...) result in a local `per_league` var, print from that, and only omit it from `out`/evaluation.json).

all_findings.title: Flask app runs with debug=True bound to 0.0.0.0 — Werkzeug debugger RCE exposed to the network
all_findings.issue: app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True) is hardcoded with no environment gating. debug=True enables the Werkzeug interactive traceback debugger, which lets a client execute arbitrary Python in the server process from the browser console on any unhandled exception (the PIN is derivable/brute-forceable and, on many setups, effectively bypassable). host="0.0.0.0" makes this reachable from every interface on the network, not just localhost, so any exception path in a route becomes a remote-code-execution surface. The reloader also runs the app as untrusted code. This is the single highest-severity issue in the codebase.
all_findings.fix: Never ship debug=True. Read it from the environment and default off, and bind to localhost by default, e.g. `app.run(host=os.getenv("HOST", "127.0.0.1"), port=int(os.getenv("PORT", "5000")), debug=os.getenv("FLASK_DEBUG") == "1")`. For any real exposure put it behind a WSGI server (gunicorn/waitress) with debug disabled.
all_findings.why_it_matters: Combined with 0.0.0.0 binding, a single unhandled exception in any route gives an attacker on the network a path to arbitrary code execution on the host.
all_findings.reason: app.py:302 is literally `app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True)`, hardcoded with no environment gating — grep of the file shows no os.getenv/os.environ usage anywhere. debug=True enables Werkzeug's interactive debugger (RCE via browser console on any unhandled exception), and host=\"0.0.0.0\" binds it to all network interfaces, not just localhost. The finding's description matches the code exactly.
all_findings.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is fine as-is: `app.run(host=os.getenv("HOST", "127.0.0.1"), port=int(os.getenv("PORT", "5000")), debug=os.getenv("FLASK_DEBUG") == "1")`, remembering to `import os` at the top of app.py if not already imported. For real deployment, run behind gunicorn/waitress with debug disabled rather than Flask's own dev server.

all_findings.title: teams_json injected into a <script> block with |safe over json.dumps — </script> breakout / XSS
all_findings.issue: `var TEAMS = {{ teams_json|safe }};` renders app.py:184's `teams_json=json.dumps(teams)` verbatim inside a <script> element. Python's json.dumps does NOT escape '<', '>', '&', or '/', so a team name containing the literal sequence '</script>' (or '<!--', ']]>') terminates the script element and injects arbitrary markup/JS into the page. Team names originate from external, non-curated CSV feeds (football-data.co.uk and the footballcsv GitHub mirror) and flow through team_stats.json into `teams`, so this is attacker-influenceable data, not a constant. Note the same file at line 135 correctly uses `|tojson` for other values, which proves the safe path is available and this one is an inconsistency.
all_findings.fix: Replace `{{ teams_json|safe }}` with `{{ teams|tojson }}` (Flask's tojson filter HTML-escapes <, >, & and is script-context safe) and drop the manual `teams_json=json.dumps(teams)` in app.py:184.
